speechtext: Mr. 0. L. BOULANGER (Bellechasse) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 18, to amend the Civil Service Act (returned soldiers' preference).
Explain.

This bill is similar to one introduced at the last session. It proposes three things. First, it is intended to restrict veterans' preference to Canadian veterans, the term Canadian being defined by the Canadian Nationals Act, chapter 21 of the revised statutes. Secondly, it proposes to extend from three to five years the requirement in regard to necessary residence in Canada demanded of applicants for positions in the civil service. In the third place, it proposes to do away with a practice which has been introduced into the administration of the Civil Service Commission regarding exceptions made to the clause requiring three years' residence in Canada for applicants. The Civil Service Commission has adopted what I might call blanket regulations, which seem to contradict the terms of the Civil Service Act, and in virtue of which applicants are admitted practically as a matter of course into the civil service without complying with the requirements of the Civil Service Act in

Whenever it may be necessary to make an exception tn the requirements of the Civil Service Act, it is proposed that such exception shall be a special case to be specially considered by the cabinet.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. J. S. W OODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 19, to amend the Criminal Code (unlawful assemblies).
Explain.

This bill is simply to provide a safeguarding clause to ensure that the general nature and character of speeches on public affairs shall be the ground for regarding any meeting as unlawful. In some of our cities recently there has been what seems to some of us an abuse of the law, whereby citizens have been prejudiced with regard to their utterances, while others who may have been listening have been declared to be members of an unlawful assembly; and this without any regard to the general character of the speeches made. This bill is merely to prevent that sort of thing in future.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: This is similar to a large number of items that will appear in these supplementary estimates. The custom grew up of carrying forward balances from one year to the other. A printing account of $25,000 at the end of last year was owing by the Civil Service Commission to the Department of Public Printing. When the estimates for the last year were made available it followed that when the balance of printing accounts for the preceding year was paid there remained just that much less money to take care of the business of the department. The result is that some $22,000 would ordinarily have been required, but owing to economies effected otherwise the amount called for to pay the balance due to the printing department to square the accounts of the commission is $20,000.

I do not know whether this is the proper time to discuss the Civil Service Commission, but I would ask the government whether it has arrived at any policy with respect to the abolition of that body. I have in my hand a report of a speech made on February 23, 1931, by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon). I will translate freely from the French. The hon. member is reported in a newspaper called Le Franc Parler, published in the city of Quebec under the auspices and with the imprimatur of the deputy speaker of the house.
That is the only controlling interest?
Wait and see.

My hon. friend says "Wait
and see." May I say that the hon. member, during the late ill fated visit to England of the right hon. Prime Minister and the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) was publicly styled in the newspapers the Acting Solicitor General. Therefore, his statement is almost an official or at least a quasiofficial statement. He says that he speaks for the members from the province of Quebec and his statement is published in a newspaper owned or at least directed by an important official of this house, the deputy speaker. I believe it is the duty of the ministers from the province of Quebec and of the Prime Minister to take the committee into their confidence in this matter. This should be done before we vote any further sums, and I ask the Prime Minister to give us this information.

Mr. Chairman, I hasten
to take the committee into my confidence. speechtext: Not unless the committee gives him permission. It is hardly in accordance with the usual sportsmanlike qualities of my hon. friend. With respect to the sneer
of the right hon. the Prime Minister-

my hon. friend's.

I accept my right hon.
friend's statement, as I must, that these are matters which should not be discussed on these estimates, but we in Quebec understood that this was an urgent matter. It is extremely unlikely that the Civil Service Commission's estimates will come up for several months. During the period which will intervene between now and the end of the session when the Civil Service Commission's estimates usually come up there will be hundreds of friends of the right hon. gentlemen, hundreds of friends of the hon. member for Dorchester, of the Solicitor General and of the Postmaster General seeking positions in the civil service but who will be precluded by the rules and regulations of the Civil Service Commission. A large number of those are my electors, some of whom up until last September were my devoted friends and on their behalf and in order that the position of the hon. gentlemen opposite may be made known to the public, in order that the people of this country outside of their constituencies as well as within may know something of the value of their statements, I think it is the duty, if the Prime Minister does not wish to do it, of members of the administration from the province of Quebec who are specifically mentioned in this article, to express their views on this matter. There should be no question about it and the people for whom I speak should know where they stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?

No; I am prepared to stay here a long time. I think the Prime Minister owes it to the house to make some statement on these estimates. We have no desire to be obnoxious, but when our friends were sitting on this side of the house we did the best we could to accommodate them in every way. My right hon. friend will not deny that we gave him and his supporters whatever information was asked for, and whatever questions were asked were answered by the ministers of the then government. I believe it is a duty, at any rate it is a courtesy, to give whatever information is asked for, and I do not believe the Prime Minister would be lacking in courtesy to hon. members. It is only in conformity with the ordinary amenities of public life that he 
should answer a question put to him in a courteous manner. I do not ask him to give a general statement as to the policy of the government, although I think I would be entitled to do so; but I ask him, if he will not speak himself, to allow his ministers, the Postmaster General, the Solicitor General, or some of his other ministers to do so. Let someone on that side of the house say in the Commons of Canada what they have been saying throughout the country. The hon. member for Dorchester, who was so bold at a banquet, should be willing to explain his views to the house. Hon. members would, I am sure, be interested; I should be much interested and if on this estimate he will move for the abolition of the Civil Service Commission, I promise him my most cordial support. I will support him to the best of my ability. There are on this side of the house a large number of members who, like him, have had to suffer from the Civil Service Commission in days gone by.
Why did you not take action in that regard yourself?

If the hon. gentleman will look up Hansard of 1923 he will find that a resolution to that effect was placed on the order paper and debated. If at that time we had had the support of hon. gentlemen opposite who to-day would be quite willing to abolish the commission, this infamous commission, composed of imbeciles, would long ago have been abolished. The question is a live one before the public. If the Prime Minister will not give an answer, the Postmaster General should give one. If he will not do so, the Solicitor General should, and if the Solicitor General will not, his deputy, the hon. member for Dorchester, ought to do this.

speechtext:
Probably no other member of the committee knows better than the hon. member for Quebec South who has just taken his seat, that even observations that are made with respect to items under consideration in the estimates, should be relevant to the question raised. He said that he did not know whether this was the appropriate place to discuss the matter or not. I think, being a member of the legal profession as he is, he will agree that neither is this the

appropriate place, nor yet can the observations be said to be relevant because they should be directed to the obtaining of information with respect to an expenditure which has been made, and regarding which we shall have something to say later as to the desirability or not of absolutely restricting expenditures to the estimates except there be cases where governor general's warrants may be issued. So far as that is concerned, anything the hon. gentleman asks shall be at once furnished him. As regards discussing the Civil Service Commission, my hon. friend can do that to his heart's content by placing a resolution on the order paper, and I look in vain to find that he has placed on the order paper a motion to have the Civil Service Commission abolished. On going into supply he has, of course, ample opportunity to mow an amendment that the house regrets that the Civil Service Commission continues to exist. All those are avenues that are open to him, but no one knows better than he that this is not thie appropriate time for such a discussion, and in the best of good nature let me say to my hon. friend that his efforts to draw his compatriots of Quebec will fail.

May I say that many of them will not be pleased to be called my compatriots. As to the appropriateness of the time, I am not disposed to enter into a discussion with the Prime Minister. He knows very well that if his prominent supporters wish to abolish the Civil Service Commission, they are quite competent to put a motion on the order paper. They could also, on the house going into committee of supply, move that the Civil Service Commission be abolished. They could, even at the present moment-and I realize I could do this myself if I so desired-follow the constitutional practice which obtains in England and with which, no doubt, the Prime Minister is familiar, of moving to reduce the estimates by one dollar. That could be done; I am glad the Prime Minister brought that matter up.

speechtext: This item does not include salaries.
That does not matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it does a great deal.
I very rarely differ from the Prime Minister on constitutional matters, but it seems to me, unless I am much mistaken, that a motion could be made to reduce this item by one dollar-to one dollar.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, to one dollar!

I am glad the Prime Minister indicated that method of procedure. Now I ask the hon. member for Dorchester to follow it. The Prime Minister has said just what he should do. The hon. member should do it before he returns to Quebec over the holidays, or I am sure he will have to find some explanation to give to the people of Quebec why he did not follow his own leader's advice and move a reduction in these estimates. It is no longer a matter of great interest to me: it is of purely academic interest to me whether the Civil Service Commission continues in existence or not. In the better days when we sat on the opposite side, I was in the habit of saying to my hon. friends that the Civil Service Commission appeared to have been created for the Tories and the Liberal back-benchers. I believe in all probability it is now created for the Tory backbenchers and the Liberals. Nobody else that I know ever seems to suffer. If the backbenchers desire to be rid of this institution, they have only to follow the method and advice laid down by the Prime Minister, and for once we promise them our hearty cooperation.

Mr. Chairman, in order to elucidate the point raised by the Prime Minister, I should like to have your ruling on the subject matter that can be discussed. I should like to call your attention first to the fact that this is the only item in these supplementary estimates where the name "Civil Service Commission" is mentioned. In the past it has been the rule of the house that when any general estimates of any department came under discussion, hon. members had the right to discuss anything that pertained to that department. I should like your ruling on the matter.

While you are considering your ruling, Mr. Chairman, may I ask the Prime Minister whether or not his government has reached a decision regarding a reorganization of several departments, and whether it is true that many employees of the civil service will lose their jobs within a short time?

speechtext: In answer to the hon. member for Rimouski, I am not here to explain the rules of the house, but if the hon. member wishes to raise a point of order, I will give him my ruling.

Do I understand, Mr. Chairman, that my question was not put politely? I was speaking in my mildest and sweetest tones to the right hon. gentleman. If there was something offensive in what I said, I have not the slightest idea what it was. I

I think, Mr. Chairman, that you have given a ruling already. The very fact that you have given that answer enables any hon. member to go on with the discussion. I am quite satisfied.

The satisfactory thing about your ruling, Mr. Chairman, is that no one has to pay the costs, and in that respect it is unlike a legal ruling. May I ask the Prime Minister once more, with all the suavity I possess, if he will be good enough to give me an answer to my question. So many civil servants and their families are very anxious to know what is going to happen with respect to their jobs, especially in these hard times. No answer? If there was something wrong with my question, I would ask the Prime Minister to tell me what it was. I cannot answer myself. Will you, Mr. Chairman, please let me know if there is no answer to my question. I am not deaf but I did not hear any answer.
The question is a joke.

It is no joke. This is a very serious matter to the civil service. We are here representing the people. We have two members in this house representing the city of Ottawa, and every other hon. member represents the country at large. We are all interested in this question. It is no good for the government to say: We are going to do this and we are going to do that; and then do nothing at all; and when something is done, it is most often wrong. I wish to be nice to the right hon. gentleman, but if he does not intend to answer me, I shall have to drop my sweet tones and speak roughly.
The hon. gentleman-

I think I know why the hon. gentleman is so cross. It is because a dark horse has won the international Bennett race for the ministry. It is very sad, Mr. Chairman. We are travelling on a mystery ship to treasure island. We know nothing, and nothing is told us. The government asks us to vote these items blindly. According to parliamentary institutions that date back to Magna Charta, the representatives of the people are entitled to know what is the policy of the government. Here we are ready to cooperate with the government in all good measures. We on this side of the house are not narrow-minded; we are broad-minded. I have sat in this house for several years on the

opposite side, and when hon. gentlemen opposite were sitting over here, never did I see a Liberal minister refuse to give them any information they desired. Very often indeed Liberal ministers have supplied Conservative members with confidential information, trusting them to keep it confidential. The Liberal ministers treated all members of the house fairly, without any distinction of party. The fiscal year ends to-morrow, Mr. Chairman, and there are many people who are anxious to know what is the policy of the government with respect to the civil service. Is the government going to give its policy to the press before advising members of the house. I would not be surprised at that at all. Am I to receive no answer? I wish to be courteous to the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues and supporters in this house, but I say that in this request for information I am backed up by all the electors of my constituency irrespective of political affiliations. Once more I ask the Prime Minister if he has anything to say regarding his policy with respect to the civil service.

I should like to get
some information from the Prime Minister in connection with this matter. There are rumours that retrenchments are to be made in the civil service, and that the employees of one department in particular, the Interior department, are to be placed elsewhere. I should like to know if, in considering the retention of employees in the service or their placement elsewhere, the government will give a preference to native-born Canadians. I am in receipt of a resolution from the Native Sons of Canada, asking that such a preference be given. I am sorry that I have not the resolution here; it is in my room, but if the Prime Minister will allow me, I will send him a copy of it. This is an influential society, which is taking a great interest in the affairs of the Dominion, and it recommends that so far as possible native-born Canadians be retained in the service in preference to non-Canadians.

Mr. Chairman-Central,
please get me a connection with the ministry! The line seems to be busy. I want to speak to the right hon. the Prime Minister. Ah, I see the line which was out of order has now been repaired and that I have the attention of the right hon. gentleman. I would ask him once more, what is the policy of the government. regarding civil service employees. This question has frequently been discussed in the press, and I would like to know what is going to happen. If the Civil Service Commission

is abolished, will all the present employees be dismissed? Will there be a complete change of staffs in the departments?
Oh, oh.

Hon. members laugh; but I am serious. The Prime Minister smiles. I like to see him smile. He is at his best then; it is the natural thing for him to do. Apparently, Mr. Chairman, the line has got out of order again. It is very sad, Mr. Chairman, to have such a disgraceful experience.
Hear, hear.

Some hon. gentlemen say, " hear, hear." It shows that they understand. They are not deaf, but they are dumb. Yes, they are dumb. La chatte leur a mange la langue. The cat has eaten their tongue; they do not speak; they have nothing to say. They think a lot; in fact they think so much they have nothing to say. Yes, they think all the time. My hon. friends opposite remind me of a very clever little boy who went to see his grandfather and spoke to him about candy.
Order.

The hon. gentleman
is wasting the time of the house.

Well, well, listen. The
little boy said: " II ne parle pas." I would say that of the right hon. the Prime Minister. I wonder if the right hon. gentleman said all he had to say during the last election campaign.
Order.

I am reminded of the
bright sunshine which follows a long period of rain. The smile of my right hon. friend might be likened to that sunshine. However we on this side of the house are just poking little jokes at him to keep him in good humour. As he is in good humour now I would like to have an answer.
Order.
Sit down.

No, I am not here to sit down. My right hon. friend knows that as soon as he gets up I will sit down. Until that time, however, I will claim my right and privilege as a member of this house to ask for all available information in the matter. To be dumb is a contagious disease, and I am afraid my hon. friends on the other side of the house are stricken with that complaint, except for purposes of heckling. They make no answer. I would like to know if an answer 22110-261
is to come. Will it come? And from where will it come? The hon. the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) who is in charge of the Civil Service Commission is not in the house and the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is piloting the estimates. I know very well that the Prime Minister must be familiar with all the details in connection with those estimates and I would be very thankful if he would tell us something about them. The silence of my hon. friends opposite reminds me of a practice which prevailed at college. When I attended school there was a period called le grand silence which extended from eight o'clock in the evening until six o'clock in the morning, and in that time nobody was allowed to speak. To-day we have a similar situation; no hon. members on the other side of the house will speak. Well, we have some doctors in the house. We have the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) who is a doctor. I wonder why he does not cure the dumbness of the Prime Minister. The hon. gentleman is a doctor and I am told he is a very good one. Then there is the hon. the Minister of Health (Mr. MadLaren) and hie is a doctor. Is it not a disease to be dumb? The hon. gentleman does not say a word. Perhaps he is suffering from that contagious disease. I think the right hon. gentleman should delegate his first medical officer in the department to cure the dumbness of all the Tories on the other side of thie house. I am pleased to bring to the attention of the Minister of Health the illness of my hon. friends opposite. No answer; wre must have Rip Van Winkle before us. La belle au bois dormant.

The question I should like to ask my right hon. friend does not relate so much to the item under consideration as to a matter of procedure, which, however, I feel might best be mentioned at this stage. Up to the present, in reference to the explanation of estimates which affect several departments of the government, we have only heard from the right hon. Prime Minister. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do I understand my right hon. friend desires by his remarks to have it inferred that the ministers who are responsible heads of the different departments are not to be expected to answer questions put to them in regard to matters affecting their departments, where these matters arise out of the estimates which are before us?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

Yes; that was the procedure followed last year when the supplementary estimates for the preceding year were submitted. These do not involve future expenditures. These are expenditures that already have been made, and I might further say to my right hon. friend that these were largely made before we came into power. The duty is cast upon me, and I think he will agree in a moment as to the soundness of the position I take, of endeavouring to ensure that every minister in his department faces the new year on April 1 without carrying forward a balance which he must pay from this year's appropriation, thereby making his appropriation deficient for the present year. I am endeavouring to do that; I believe it is sound business, and if I might anticipate what I am going to say in a moment, the Auditor General points out that that should be done. I brought with me the volume of the Auditor General's report containing that recommendation. In his report for the year ending March 31, 1930, at page

In the year 1928-29 the carry over was $1,572,000, and last year it was $505,000, so there was $1,000,000 appropriated for the current year that had to go for the purpose of paying the accounts of the past year. As these estimates are of that character I assumed that the usual practice of the Minister of Finance, who is responsible for the passage of the supply bill, of making explanations, would be the proper one to follow, and I was going to make a little more lengthy explanation in connection with this matter and ask the committee to agree with me that there should be no over expenditure in the different departments. 'Certainly the right does not exist in any department to over expend money through the officials when there has been no appropriation by parliament. I should think that principle has been clearly laid down, although it has been departed from in some instances without the ministers knowing about it. The time has come when some very drastic action will have to be taken to prevent a recurrence of that condition.

The present session opened rather late and we are already in the midst of our spring operations. Unless I am very much mistaken, during the last ten years hon. members have had the right to discuss the general policy adopted by any department at the time their estimates were being considered, no matter whether it was an item which had been spent or otherwise. I do not desire to embarrass the Prime Minister, but in view of the lateness of the opening of the session and the disappointment of the farmers at receiving nothing of a definite character, after having been prepared for a pronouncement by the Prime Minister at the Regina meeting, a statement of policy should be made by the government. I am making this suggestion in fairness to the people whom I represent and who are very vitally interested in the agricultural policy of this government. I do not claim that governments can do everything for the farmer or for the unemployed, but at the same time these people are expecting something. If we have nothing to give them, let them know it so that they can act accordingly.

This committee, being anxious to retain some semblance of integrity with respect to its dealings, is now legalizing the unwarranted acts of those who made certain expenditures because they say they were instructed to do so. In my judgment, that is a wrong conception of their public duties by the permanent officials of this country. I am seeking to do only what I think any minister in my place would endeavour to do as Minister of Finance charged with the responsibility of a supply bill-to deal with these items without any undue delay. The responsibility is, as the Auditor General says, with the accountants of the departments, and if parliamentary control of appropriations is to be maintained except under very exceptional conditions that may sometimes prevail, it follows that discipline must be applied, or the whole system will be wrecked for if accountants and deputy ministers under the control of ministers may make, beyond parliamentary appropriations, expenditures amounting to $1,000,000, they can do it to the amount of So,000,000 or $10,000,000. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

In speaking a moment ago, I agreed with my right hon. friend as to the desirability of having the closest kind of control exercised in order to prevent government officials from sanctioning over-expenditures. What I should like to point out to him is that with respect to the expenditures we are now discussing he has had that control for eight months; the previous government had it for four months. If there is a very large excess of expenditure, my right hon. friend and his ministers are the ones who are primarily responsible for it; they have had the control at the time when its exercise was required. Moreover, I am quite sure, although I have not had an opportunity to secure the estimates, that if we look back for many years in the past, we shall find that the item which is now before the committee is one that has appeared regularly in the supplementary estimates. It does not arise solely from over-payments in the current fiscal

year. As my right hon. friend said a moment ago, there are many things which are unforeseen, items that even deputy ministers and ministers have not foreseen and the Auditor General has not foreseen. In a business involving the expenditure of between $300,000,000 and $400,000,000 annually, it would be extraordinary if there were not items here and there running into a few thousand dollars that might escape notice in that way. This item is inserted to make good those unforeseen amounts. It need not imply any real neglect on the part of anyone unless it is carried to too great an extreme.

My right hon. friend will find as he continues his administration, that with a great many contracts unfinished, it is very difficult to end a year with a complete payment of accounts covering that particular year. Provision is made for a short period in which to cover those accounts. I am quite well aware of the practice spoken of by my right hon. friend, but may I point out to him that the Auditor General is the individual who is in charge and who has control and can control.

speechtext:
No. There may be a
small sum. My right hon. friend says that it was $2,055,000 odd for the year 1921-22. It was $1,500,000 in 1928-29.
The Auditor General directs attention to what must be painfully apparent to everyone. It means that you substitute the minister and an accountant for parliament, because the money has gone and there was no appropriation for it. Instead of doing what I might have done, namely, let this be treated as a supplementary estimate next year, or in the supplementary estimates this year by putting in an item "to cover amount unprovided for",
I am giving the details of each department where the overdraft was, so there might be upon the record an indication of what these overdrafts were, and then we would start fair and square with the world. That is what has been done. The question as to policy cannot enter it because I could abandon all these items and treat them simply as one item, as was done in the main estimates. But I am going to endeavour at least-one may fail in the endeavour; an ex-minister says that we will fail, but I do not thing that we will-to see that hereafter there mil be no over-expenditures by accountants and deputy ministers in departments, with the aid of a minister, about which the minister may know nothing-
Except under governor general's warrant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Exactly, but that is another thing altogether. Then those over expenditures are legalized in the estimates that come before the house. Once more I desire to make it clear to the committee, although it may be that my conception of my obligations as Minister of Finance is not such that I shall be able to realize it-the hon. member for West Edmonton says that is so-
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But this is so. We are asking the committee this afternoon to pass these estimates of money that has been expended so that this house may hold this administration responsible for what happens from tihe 1st day of April next, after which we cannot say that any part of the expenditures were incurred by the former administra-
Supply-Unprovided Items

tion. I think an effort should be made to make it possible for each department to live within its appropriation. If not, some men will lose their positions. That is all I have to say.

Would the minister be kind enough to elucidate one point. He says that these expenditures have been incurred by different departments, but that no payments have been made. The expenditures were authorized but no payments were made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In many instances the
payments have been made in full.

Speaking from
experience, I would say that some of the statements that have been made by my right hon. friend are not exactly-I do not like to use the word, correct-but I remember when I was deputy minister, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) whom I had the honour of having as my minister at one time will bear me out in this-never was any overexpenditure of that kind authorized. The expenditure may have been incurred, but no payments were made before the appropriation was voted. I think that applies in this case also, unless there were extraordinary payments that I am not aware of.
Another thing: In every department, before the accountant or even the deputy minister .can authorize any over-payment of that kind, the Auditor General must sanction that overpayment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He says not.
He is making a mistake, because in my experience as deputy minister never has an accountant paid out a check without getting the authority of the Auditor General. That is provided by law.
I think my right hon. friend must be under a misapprehension because there are cases where an appropriation is exhausted, and then either the account must stand until the money is voted or-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what they do not do.

Where do
they get the money?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With an overdraft.
I never was able to get it except by a governor general's warrant. My right hon. friend will find that the accounting situation is not quite so loose as he would depict it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would just answer my hon. friend by saying that his own department owed the printing bureau a large sum

of money, which we had to pay, thereby reducing by that amount the grant that was available for the purpose indicated. The printing bureau rendered their accounts promptly, and there was no reason why these accounts should not have been paid; but by not paying them you got past the passing of the estimate, and showed just that much less money to vote. If you wish to go on in that way, that is all that it is necessary to do. But the liability has to be met another year. T

I am not
questioning that at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let me give the figures. There was over three-quarters of a million dollars owing to the printing department by different departments. Part of that was in consequence of the election, the same as the census vote, which is a large item, but matters of that kind can be dealt with and should be dealt with. My hon. friend says that the Auditor General passes upon the account. All I can say is that he says not.
feir riUGENE FISET: He is a new man; he has been imposed upon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not see how the
Auditor General necessarily sees the accounts before they are paid. He does not know the
sum total. All he passes on is the accuracy of the account.
hir EUGENE FISET: In my department there was pre-audit, a continuous audit, and a post-audit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is not sufficient to enable him to say whether the appropriation is exhausted. He says in his report:
As pointed out on page V of my report for last year, the responsibility for these overexpenditures rests entirely with the departments administering the appropriations exceeded and especially with the accountants of the departments, whose duties in such cases are clearly defined.
And then the order in council is given. Since I have been in the Department of Finance I have observed that to be the case and to the best of my ability I have endeavoured and purpose to continue to provide that there will be no over expenditures next year beyond the appropriations.

Will the right hon. gentleman allow me to make one more remark? During the war and even while demobilization appropriations were being made my hon. friend will remember that under the War Appropriation Act the audit was changed to fhe extent of allowing the Auditor General to take charge of audits of the expenditures

Supply-Unprovided Items
made by the Department of Militia and Defence. I am more familiar with those expenditures than with the expenditures of the department about which my right hon. friend is talking at the present time. I know however that there is a provision in the audit act that every accountant before incurring any expenditure not voted by parliament absolutely must consult the Auditor General.

I would like to ask
the Prime Minister a question. Are we to understand that these supplementary estimates are being asked to cover a deficit for which this government is not responsible? Have new policies for which this government is not responsible brought about some of these expenditures? Take for instance the subject of agriculture.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not use the word deficit generally as perhaps the hon. member will follow. I used the word deficit in respect to appropriations in every instance, and the details are given with much greater fullness than has usually been the case. Instead of putting in the supplementary estimates for the whole account under one item we pursued the other course and gave to the committee details of every department as to contemplated expenditures. Some of the expenditures represent a continuation of policies and some of them represent sums already expended. I give the following illustration. We will suppose that the grant is 1600 and the expenditure is $700 but exactly the same policy has been followed at which involved the spending of only $600. Extraordinary circumstances however involved the necessity of increasing the expenditure to $700 and we have asked for a supplementary estimate because the money has 'been paid. I will say to my hon. friend the ex-Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence that in many instances the money has not been paid. In the major number of instances however it has been paid. Despite what the hon. member thinks should have been the practice, and with him I agree, the Auditor General has said it is not the practice and as he is Charged with the responsibility I am bound to accept his interpretation and I think my hon. friend will agree there has been no mistake made in the matter so far as I am concerned.
I was merely asking for information.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The right hon. the Prime Minister has given to the house as an explanation of the $2,055,000 unprovided
item in the accounts of 1921-1922 the fact that the amount was due to special grants for the unemployed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The years 1922 and 1923.
No, 1921-22. I quote-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I thought the right hon. gentleman said 1922 and 1923.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No. My right hon. friend had the book before him, and it shows an unprovided item for 1921-22. The sum mentioned is to cover unprovided items for the years 1921-22 as per the Auditor General's report part b, page 3. I have that part of the report in my hand and I will read from it in order to explain how the unprovided items arose. The grant for agriculture was exceeded by $12.72. The charges of management grant was exceeded by $3,08831; civil government salaries, by $5,416.95; civil government contingencies by $507.22; customs and inland revenue by $167,705.67 and demobilization by $976,322.89.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the item to which I referred.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, demobilization. But that does not account for a million dollars; the amount to which my right hon. friend referred was over $2,000,000. Then, in connection with militia and defence the grant was exceeded by $2,999.14. The grant for penitentiaries was exceeded by $161,738.24; that for pensions by $298,428.06; for post office, outside service $417,93529; for public works, income, $20,510.36; for the collection of revenue, S350.84; for trade and commerce, $15.17; making a total of $2,055,030.86. If we deduct the amount my right hon. friend had in mind, that for demobilization amounting to $976,322.89, there is still left over $1,055,000 of grant exceeded which appeared as unprovided items for the years 1921-22. That was a period during which hon. gentlemen opposite had been in office for nine months and the Liberal administration in office for three months. The item we have this year arises when a Liberal administration has been in office for four months and hon. gentlemen opposite have had control for eight months. It is not the figure of $2,055,000 but the figure of $505,000. I would ask the house and the country to draw their own conclusion.

I do not wish to leave my hon. friend under a misapprehension that I have made the statement that there was absolute control. I agree that perhaps more control is desirable. In departments there is such a thing as switching votes,
Supply-Unprovided, Items

and that practice should I think be prohibited. It should not be practised to any considerable degree. I do wish to say to him however that never in my nine years experience have I known the department to pay by cheque out of an appropriation that was exhausted. That is what would have to happen before a supplementary would be required. May I say to my right hon. friend that that cannot be done. Either money would have to be provided by warrant or the practice would have to be adopted to which my right hon. friend has taken exception, the practice of allowing it to run over into the next year and paying it out of the appropriation for the following year. I will admit that has been practised but not to any great extent. I think however that is a practice which might very well be stopped at once and permanently.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
All I can say is that the Auditor General has used this expression:
"the over expending of appropriations." . . . and it can mean only one thing.

I do not
question that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-has the effect of lessening parliamentary control over expenditures and although in very exceptional cases it may have to be permitted, the practice is to be deprecated and means should be taken to prevent it.
That is the statement made by the Auditor General.
He does not refer to payments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In some cases payments have actually been made.
That is the point to which we take exception.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I believe we are not so
much at variance. I see the point taken by my hon. friend. The Department of the Interior owes the printing department several hundred thousand dollars. Instead of paying that amount between the end of March and the first of May, thereby incurring an extension of the estimates to that extent, payment was not made. As soon as the estimates are voted however payment is made. That decreases the amount of money available for the estimates.
That undoubtedly is what happens all along the line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Hon. members will find
amounts passed by this house against which I protested to the extent of three-quarters of a million dollars. In tracing the matter

I have found that practice has been followed right through the piece. The Secretary of State approaches various departments and and asks for money to which they reply that they have no money, the money having been used for some other purpose, namely to pay deficits of the year before. If that is what the hon. gentleman means then we are one.

There is no doubt that is what has happened. I do not question that, but what I do question is the statement of my hon. friend. Those moneys we are now voting could not be paid unless my hon. friend had warrants for them, and all the warrants that have been passed are here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They have nothing to
do with these things.

The
amounts for which you are now asking the consent of parliament will have to be paid after the appropriations are made.
Mr. BENNETT [DOT] My information is that they have been paid, and the Auditor General says so.
They could not have been paid unless the Auditor General allowed them to switch accounts. There is no other way in which it could be done.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Agriculture - publications - further amount required, $3,000.

May I ask the Prime
Minister just what publications are referred to here?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Publications of the
Department of Agriculture, brochures with respect to weeds, seeds, livestock and so on for which the appropriation last year was $28,000. They required $31,000, a considerable part of which was incurred by reason of the fact that a new office was being occupied, and the movement of the publications entailed considerable expense.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Pensions-salaries and contingent expenses; of the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada-further amount required, $40,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This represents a sum. for which parliament made no appropriation last session, and which was expended for the purpose of setting up the tribunals under the-statute passed Last year. There is one chief counsel at $4,000 per annum; seven assistant counsels at $3,600 per annum; one junior

Supply-Welland Canal
solicitor at $2,640; two clerks, grade four, at $1,680 each, and a medical staff consisting of one assistant medical adviser at $4,020; four pensions medical examiners at $3,040; one stenographer, grade two and four additional stenographers, making a total of $59,420. Then there are travelling expenses and the subsistence for six months amounting to $12,600. The total of the items I gave is $59,420, and $40,000 further is required to take care of the service.

I think this amount is put in the estimates under a misnomer. It is said to cover salaries and contingent expenses of the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada, but the Prime Minister in his explanation tells us that the money is required for the establishment of the tribunals, which is an entirely different thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Board of Pension Commissioners is the designation under which this is all classed.

No, the Board of Pension Commissioners is the standing board, and this amount is required for the tribunals. I think it is a mistake.
Mr. POWEiR: I think that item should be divided; that portion which has to do with commission counsel might apply to the Board of Pension Commissioners, while the remainder should be credited to the Department of Pensions and National Health.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite correct as to the item covering two services, the commission service and the medical staff. The medical staff which I gave is under George V, chapter 35, section 1051, and (the other is under sections 1, 2 and 3 of the same statute, with respect to commission counsel. The one amounts to $23,820 and the other to $35,600.
Perhaps by adding the words "and staff" it might be sufficient,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It has been all treated in the Auditor General's accounts up to the moment as part of the Board of Pension Commissioners. The setting up of the new tribunals has been carried for the moment in that classification, but the appropriations will be separate in the main estimate which provides for that work. This, I understand, is sufficient to take care of the deficit.
Will the right hon. gentleman give us the names of the solicitors who have been appointed, together with the salary in each case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have given the salaries.
I have not the names at the moment. These items will all be revoted in the main estimates.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Railways and Canals-Welland ship canal; construction and betterments-further amount required, $2,000,000.
The Prime Minister gave a short explanation in connection with this matter some time ago. Would he mind repeating that explanation now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I should be very glad to do so. The construction of the Welland ship canal, as the committee well knows, is being done under contract. It is usual, weather conditions being as they are, that the work stops at a certain season of the year and is resumed in the spring. Having regard to unemployment conditions, the minister authorized the contractors, who employ several thousand men, to continue their work, it being well understood that this did not increase the cost to the country. They continued their work and gave employment during the winter, but they were informed they would not be paid until parliament made new provision accordingly, and this item is to enable that to be done.

Then this is at least
$2,000,000 for which the old government is not responsible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so; I did not suggest that at all.
I am not quite sure that I understood the explanation of the Prime Minister. Am I to understand that the contractors were paid an extra amount to have them carry on the work later in the season?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No agreement was made to pay them extras, but they were asked to continue the service in view of the fact that a large number of men were unemployed. They have not been paid. This is a case in which they have not been paid, and they were told they could not be paid until provision was made for that purpose.

But I understand certain sums of money were voted last year for the Welland canal. Tenders must have been called for and contracts let. Am I to gather from what the Prime Minister has said that these contracts were extended to cover more work, larger quantities of work, or that the units of work were extended?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The total estimate last year was $7,600,000 and it was anticipated that between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000 would be
Supply-Welland, Canal

spent. As a matter of fact more than that was spent, and this $2,000,000 is to take care of that sum, which will be available after March 31. That is, they merely 'had a contract and went ahead with it. There was no money in the estimates to take care of this expenditure.
It was really an additional contract which was given, then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, just the same contract.
The same contract, but more work was performed than was anticipated at the time the contract was let.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The engineers of the Department of Railways and Canals had estimated that the contractors, who have a contract to continue the work to completion, would spend in the neighbourhood of seven million dollars last year. But the weather was so fine, the fall was so open that the contractors had finished that portion of the work for which the seven million dollars was appropriated and would then be obliged to lay off their men. It was in September some time, and the question was whether we should tell them to go on and wait for the passing of this estimate by the house, or allow them to lay off two thousand men.
The unit prices were the same?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.
Just what period was covered by the work represented by this extra two million dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We figured it would take two million dollars up to March 31, and when
this estimate is passed the contractors will get their money.
How much more money will be devoted to the Welland canal? How far has the work progressed?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The work is obviously progressing rapidly or we would not spend the extra two million dollars.
How many more millions do you want?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There is a requirement of about seven or eight million dollars-in the neighbourhood of seven million dollars-to complete the work. Whether it will be all completed this year or not is not known at the present time.
As I understand it, under ordinary conditions this work would have closed down at a certain period-

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is not quite right.

-and the appropriation voted last session would have been sufficient to carry on the work up to that period. Owing either to the open season or to the necessity for carrying the work along further than ordinarily, with a view to relieving unemployment, the contractors were authorized to go on with their operations, which would represent an expenditure beyond the appropriation voted last session. In view of that permission given them to go beyond that appropriation, and naturally supposing that, it being out of the ordinary, the work might cost the contractors more per unit at that advanced season of the year, has the department obligated itself to the contractors to pay them anything additional beyond the unit prioes of the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
None whatever. May I
point out that my hon. friend's premise is wrong. Under ordinary circumstances, with ordinary weather conditions, the amount of $7,000,000 voted last year would have taken care of the work until the freeze-up. But because the weather was so fine, the season so open, the freeze-up being delayed, the contractors could carry on their work further than they otherwise would have been able to do. Consequently they got through more expeditiously than they had anticipated the work which they had estimated to do this year, and rather than allow them to lay off a couple of thousand men in strenuous times we permitted the contractors to continue operations on the condition that they would not be paid until the estimate was passed by the house. It makes no difference whatever, except that there was performed this year rcork which, under ordinary weather conditions, would have been held over.

Suppose we had had the
ordinary freeze-up, this work would not have been carried on?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is right.

I claim that there has been the ordinary freeze-up, to use that term. It has not been as early in the season as heretofore, but there has been a freeze-up and these men have carried on work after that freeze-up.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Not the part interfered
with by the freeze-up. They got a good proportion of the work done earlier because the freeze-up was so late, but certain other works they were in a position to carry on.

Supply-Welland Canal

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Prime
Minister has been speaking of the desirability of controlling expenditures by the government. A fundamental principal is that when parliament votes money for a particular purpose that appropriation should be used exclusively for that purpose, and if a further appropriation is necessary the ministry may take one of two courses: It may ask parliament to vote the further appropriation, or, if parliament is not in session, it may secure from His Excellency a governor general's warrant, should the work be urgent, and the additional expenditure be justified on that ground. The minister has told us that this work was continued in order, as I understand it, to give employment to men who otherwise would have been unemployed. The minister says so. That being the case, I submit that the government should have adopted one of two courses. It might have taken a part of the appropriation which this parliament made for the purpose of relieving unemployment-the $20,000,000-and used it to provide employment in some such way. I am not so sure, there being a contract already in existence, that it would have been wholly proper for the government to do it in that way. But at least there was money voted for unemployment purposes under that specific heading. As an alternative, however, had the matter been one of great necessity, the government might have done what apparently they have done in other cases; they might have secured a governor general's warrant for the necessary amount. But they had no right whatever, of their own accord, to issue contracts to contractors for work to be done on the Welland canal or for anything else without this parliament having in the first instance made the requisite appropriation. In this instance the government has taken upon itself to spend $2,000,000 without having a governor general's warrant for the purpose, or without having an appropriation from parliament. I say that is an entirely wrong method of procedure, and if the Prime Minister is anxious, as apparently he is, to reform the methods of controlling expenditures, he had better begin immediately with his own colleagues and his own administration.

Mr. Speaker, evidently, this amount of $2,000,000 has been spent to relieve the unemployed in the province of Ontario. That is discrimination. The government has no right to have parliament appropriate $2,000,000, for Ontario, over and above the $20,000,000 voted for all the provinces, in the course of the emergency session.
I repeat it, that is discrimination. I think parliament should refuse to vote this amount. Moreover, why should Ontario be more favoured than the other provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is well to correct a misstatement on the part of my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King). There was no new contract; the contracts were made by the right hon. gentleman's government. They are contracts that will have to be paid The contractors had exhausted the money voted, and the only question was whether or not they should go on-because they will have to be paid anyway. It makes no difference; they will have to be paid under that contract which the former government made and which we could not break. The only question, therefore, was whether or not they should continue the work instead of laying off the men, as would ordinarily be done. It was the question between discontinuing the work or allowing the men to get the benefit of employment during the still open season. We said, "We have no money to pay you because the government, anticipating the requirements, provided what they thought necessary for the purpose." And the money not being ample to carry on the additional work performed by the contractors under their contract-it was not a new contract but the same one-we allowed them to continue operations on the understanding that they would finance the work themselves and when parliament met, as it was bound to do, the necessary appropriation would be passed. Parliament had to do it anyway.
They could have carried on under the general estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They did carry on under the general estimates, but the money was exhausted.
I mean, they could have carried on under the general estimates for the current year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. It was thought desirable to let the house know what was spent instead of carrying forward into the next year a deficit or over-expenditure on the past year's operations. This committee is being told exactly what the situation is-that $2,000,000 has been spent.
Told afterwards.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but it was under the contract which my hon. friend's government made and which had to be paid anyway.

Supply-Welland Canal
Only as regards that item which was voted last year. Parliament did not pass on the $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, but it is not referable to any item; the contract covers the work which is to go on from year to year. Money was voted to pay the contractors based upon the contemplated amount of work to be done. That amount of work was finished and then the contractors, having their machinery and plant on the ground, said that they could go along with the work and an appropriation could be put in the estimates. They wanted to know whether they would go ahead or stop work, and we said:	Go ahead and do it.

Why not put it in the
general estimates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not put in the general estimates-
I am speaking on the question of unemployment and I think I am in order. Money was voted by this house and tenders were called for but contracts were never let.
The same thing applies to British Columbia.
The same thing applies also to Quebec.

The attention of the
Minister of Labour was called to the fact that unemployment was very acute in Cara-quet and Little Shippigan and the government was asked to go on with its work. That work has not been proceeded with and no relief for unemployment has been accorded to the people in those sections. In this instance, $2,000,000 is being .expended, although no appropriation has been made, in order to relieve unemployment in some other section of Canada.

The important fact is how much the government of the day asked parliament to appropriate, and the point which comes up for consideration now is how much the government opposite, of its own volition, has incurred by way of public expenditure by order in council, without any authority from parliament and without any warrant from His Excellency, The Governor General.
