speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The item under discussion is No. 18, harbours and rivers, $440,025.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think I had given a
full explanation of this when the committee rose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Can my right
hon. friend tell us what payments have already been made within the present fiscal year on account of harbour improvements at Port Arthur and Fort William, and when the last payment was made? I understand that the item of $288,530 which appears in this estimate is for payment to be made on work that has been done in this fiscal year but for which there was not available money under the original appropriation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is correct. This
case perhaps very clearly illustrates something which my right hon. friend has overlooked, and it becomes essential to take a few moments to clear the situation. In every appropriation of public moneys tenders are usually called for and a contract is entered into. The contract involves, on the part of
the crown, the payment of the price agreed upon and, on the part of the contractor, the performance of the service which he undertakes. There is usually in all such contracts a date within which the work is to be completed, and if the contractor finishes the work within the time that is all that can reasonably be expected. But if by pushing the work forward with expedition, he anticipates the conclusion of the contract, it sometimes follows that he is in a position to get his money before he would otherwise receive it, provided that parliament has made an appropriation. If not, he has to wait until the session of parliament before he can receive it. It would be entirely wrong to grant governor general's warrants in a case such as that. Warrants are not issued where contracts have been outstanding. That has been the general principle of governments, because it has been held that the necessity which justifies the issue of a warrant does not arise where there is a contract. That principle has generally governed, although it has been departed from in some cases; for instance, it has happened where there has been a great disaster or any occurrence of that kind, even although there has been a contract, where a particular work has been destroyed. This case amply illustrates the point I was making. The contract was No. 15914, the original amount $472,500, and the contractors Messrs. Chambers, McQuigge & McCaffrey, the date of the contract, September 19, 1928, and the date for completion, July 28, 1930. I wish the committee to bear in mind that the contract was to have been completed by the middle of July last year. The contractor commenced work in September, 1928. This was authorized by order in council passed on August 26, 1928. The work was awarded to the lowest tender. There follows in the particulars I have a description of the work that was done. It was done on the unit basis. In a letter dated October 8, 1930, the minister authorized Messrs. Chambers, McQuigge & McCaffrey to proceed under the terms of their present contract with supplying and placing of core stone and cover stone in the prolongation of the section of the breakwater next adjacent to the section then under contract. This authority was given partly to relieve unemployment in Port Arthur, and was to expire at the end of the working season, the contractors to wait payment and the government to ask parliament at its next session to provide the necessary funds. The above additional work was covered by authority of order in council dated January 28, 1931, after it was known exactly how much work had been performed. The additional expenditure incurred by the

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
above authority amounted to $219,225. The total amount owing the contractors is $254,30S. That is the situation with respect to that item.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is the contract finished?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the work was finished. There is no contract outstanding for further work.
Inside the estimate?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, not quite, but the
difference is not substantial. The amount is about $35,000. There is a balance owing to the Great Lakes Dredging & Contracting Company in connection with the same work. The amount of the final estimate is $62,146.37, the amount paid being $32,177.25; the balance remaining is therefore $29,969.12. The original work under this contract consisted of certain operations which I need not mention. The work was extended on September 19, 1930, to include an additional 100,000 cubic yards from lot 10 at the confluence of the Kaministikwia river and Mission river to give more room for steamers to turn, on condition that the contractor would await payment until further funds had been voted by parliament. I mentioned this in parliament last September, when I made reference to these matters.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the Prime Minister to this point. In a number of localities where there has been public work either contemplated or commenced, the work has been stopped and there has been unemployment. Communications have been sent to the government asking whether it would be possible to have the work proceeded with and replies have been sent by the government to the effect that parliament has not made an appropriation beyond a certain amount and that it would therefore be altogether unlawful to proceed with the work. One case was mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Provencher. That was a case in point. Either this reason is a true one or it is not true; either the condition given in that reply should apply in all cases or it should apply in none. What appears to have been the case here is that in some localities where there have been contracts certain contractors have received, as it were, special favours; they have been allowed to go ahead with the work. They have been given to all intents and purposes new contracts, although they have been told that they would have to wait until parliament reassem-

bled in order to have the money voted to make good what would have to be paid to labour. On the other hand, where other communities have asked that a similar course be adopted, they have been told that it was illegal to proceed in that way. One way must be right and the other wrong, and I submit that the right way is to limit the work to the amount - parliament has voted for the contract. I recall several of the contracts which relate to items in the supplementary estimates as having been fully and carefully discussed by the previous government. It was recognized that it might not be possible to have the work completed within the fiscal year, but it was contemplated that it would be continued in the next year. My right hon. friend will, I am sure, agree that when he brings down his main estimate there will be item after item which will read somewhat in this way: To complete work, amount required in addition to-mentioning the previous amount voted. That is the way in which estimates are presented to parliament. A given work or service may involve the expenditure of $1,000,000, and the minister in presenting the estimates to the house will inform the house that while the work when completed will amount to $1,000,000, nevertheless the government is asking only for $500,000 for what is to be done within the fiscal year. The estimate for the additional $500,000, or a portion of it, will appear in the estimates of the next year. That is the way estimates are voted when voted regularly, and I submit again that wherever a departure is made from that course it is irregular.
The Prime Minister has explained to us that this expenditure was made in part to relieve unemployment. That is part of the explanation which he has put on the record. Again I would point out that parliament at the last special session voted $20,000,000 to aid in unemployment. If it was contemplated that these public works would be continued beyond the point at which it was intended by the previous administration that they should be continued, in order to provide work for the unemployed, then hon. gentlemen opposite should have submitted additional estimates at the special session, and have stated at the special session that there was going to be so much unemployment during the coming winter, that they intended to go further with the dredging of harbours, the extension of wharves and the building of public buildings than had been contemplated by the previous administration. The estimates should have been submitted to parliament and we should have been told that they were for the purpose of relieving unemployment. That would have been

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
treating parliament fairly and the public fairly, but the present method is highly irregular and is not at all defensible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad the right hon. gentleman made that closing [DOT]observation, for it enables me to point out to the committee that at the special session, on September 10,
I directed attention to that particular policy as being the policy which the government would pursue. The words I used on that occasion, which appear on page 68 of Hansard, were as follows:
Work is being carried on in connection with the breakwater, we will say. at the head of the lakes-I give that as an illustration-the parliamentary appropriation has been exhausted; the work could be usefully carried on, and give employment to several hundred men for several weeks longer; it would be proposed, at the same unit cost, to continue that work.
And on September 11 I made the following remarks, which appear on page 94 of Hansard:
But, as I said yesterday, it is proposed to continue existing contracts upon the unit basis upon which they have been let by my hon. friends opposite, in cases where by so doing employment will be provided which might not otherwise be available. And I gave an illustration. It happened to be the illustration of a breakwater which had been brought to my attention. That is, the appropriation for the year is exhausted. The work was let by tender on a unit basis.
Employment could be given to a few hundred men from now until the close of navigation by continuing the present contractors in their work under the same unit basis. That I conceive to be a proper case to deal with, and I mention it as one of those it was proposed to deal with.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. We were asked many questions as to how we proposed to deal with this problem, and we replied that we proposed to extend the docks, for instance, upon a unit basis, and we have done so. There is a clear distinction and there should be no difficulty in the committee's deciding between what is new contract and what is the continuance of existing contract. Had the work at the head of the lakes been terminated the equipment would have been removed. It was admitted that at some time or other this rock breakwater would have to be extended, and the unit cost of the work was fixed by the contract. The equipment being on the ground, the work was extended on the basis of the same unit cost as had prevailed in the original contract.
Some of the matters mentioned this afternoon involved the voting of money for new contracts, and I am sure that when we come to the main estimates my right hon. friend
will admit that no government he has ever known has succeeded in extending to the same extent the contracts of the former administration. Case after case will be found where tenders were called for and contracts let for the very reason mentioned by the right hon. gentleman, namely, to endeavour to provide employment for those who might not otherwise be usefully engaged. Many of these cases involved constituencies which had not supported the present administration, and when the main estimates are considered I feel satisfied that hon. members will admit that this government has been extraordinary in that regard. We did not do as has been done at times-cancel contracts on accession to power. A few days before the late government gave up its seals of office they passed many orders in council accepting tenders.
After defeat.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No effort was made to
cancel those contracts. How unlike the action taken by the former administration. They came into office and found that the Journal Publishing Company had leased a portion of its office space to the Agriculture department. The Auditor General's department decided that other quarters should be found and the contract was cancelled, with a resulting cost to the country of $22,000 in damages and costs. I think it will be found that a very earnest effort has been made by the officials in charge of these contracts to meet in every sense the public necessity rather than to serve any political ends.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My right hon. friend has referred to a certain contract and has tried to have it appear that with respect to contracts his government has acted differently from the previous administration. Might I remind the committee that with respect to that particular contract, and other contracts which were dealt with similarly, they were dealt with in the manner in which they were for a very obvious reason; the administration which had been in office prior to the time at which the action was taken was an administration that had never received any authority to act, either from this parliament or from the people of this country. It was a phantom administration which came into being for a short time in 1926 without having the support of the majority of this House of Commons or of the electorate of the country.
That is quite, different.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When that so-called shadow government undertook to award
contracts to its friends, ilt became a first duty
Supply-Agriculture

of the incoming administration to see that contracts of the character should not be permitted to continue. What my right hon. friend in continuing existing contracts describes as being such a virtuous act upon his part in contrast to what was done by other administrations is in reality nothing of the kind. In regard to what his administration has done in continuing the contracts which were in existence when they came into office, it will be found that in each case tenders had been called for before the elections. Moneys had been appropriated by parliament at a previous session, in all particulars the authority of parliament had been obtained, and the government which held office at the time these contracts were signed simply performed an executive act necessary to complete the will of parliament in regard to these contracts. There is nothing there for which my right hon friend is to be specially thanked.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This vote is required, first, to meet grants to fairs and expenditures in connection therewith, $19,300. Of this amount, $6,000 is needed for four new fairs named by the late administration to receive class B grants, namely Chilliwack, Armstrong, Assiniboine and Waterloo. It might be mentioned that these four fairs were named as B fairs during the elections but that has no reference to the fact that they were deserving. The fair at Valleyfield was changed from class A to class B at an increased cost of $3,500. A winter fair was started at Sherbrooke at a cost of $9,800.
In the cattle division, the amount voted for cow testing service was $55,000 while the total estimated expenditure for the year was $62,500. This is not an abnormal increase, as I think hon. gentlemen opposite will agree that when you are dealing with a matter of $55,000, an increase of $7,500 is not out of the way.
The poultry item is the largest of those I am reading. The total expenditure was in round figures $290,000. The appropriation, as will be noticed is $258,000. The departmental officials observe that the increased expenditure is due mainly to the following reasons:
1. Very greatly increased activity in poultry promotion in Quebec, in cooperation with the provincial department. In all, six new poultry promoters were added to the staff and the sum of $3,000 was set aside to assist in cokerel distribution.
TMr. Mackenzie King.]
2. The increase in the work of car-lot inspection of dressed poultry in the western provinces, an increase of easily 30 per cent. In this work, fifteen additional men were employed over the previous year. Further, the period in which the men were employed was considerably longer than in previous years, owing to the increased number of killing and plucking demonstrations and the fact that many points w'ere induced to ,ship itheir poultry earlier than previously.
For sheep work there is a deficit of $15,000. For sheep promoters the amount voted was $34,000 and the amount expended $42,000, leaving a deficit of $8,000. During the year, the increased demand for pure bred rams, increase in the organization of sheep clubs, increased demand for ewe lambs for breeding purposes, for sheep demonstrations, including demonstrations on wool, docking, castration, dipping and the control of sheep parasites necessitated increased travelling on the part of officers connected with this work. For the ram premium policy the amount voted was $10,000, the amount expended $17,000, leaving a deficit of $7,000.
As I said this afternoon, these policies were not those of the present administration. These items are but carrying out new policies as regards which I am bound in fairness to say the exact amount that would be spent could not with definiteness be ascertained, but the appropriations made were regarded as being sufficient for the purposes. A somewhat larger sum was actually expended.
The vote for the general grant was $10,000 and the expenditure slightly over $37,000, made us as follows:

Supply-Agriculture

The Prime Minister stated that there were four class B fairs for which $1,500 each is required, and I believe he said that that indebtedness was incurred by the former administration. We have in western Canada some class B fairs which were discriminated against by. the former administration. I happen to know of one particular fair, that of Kindersley, Saskatchewan, which is a class B fair on a par with those which have received the $1,500 each, yet the Kindersley fair has never yet been paid the $1,500. I believe there are two or three others similarly situated. While I know there is not much hope of receiving redress under this item, this discrimination should cease. There is absolutely no reason why one particular district in Canada should be given $1,500 of federal money while another district similarly situated is refused. I believe the present administration wants to be fair, and in fairness to all the districts, when this apportionment is made for the ensuing year, I trust that those which have been discriminated against will be included in the grant to class B fairs.

Might I point out to
the administration that there are two classes of class B fairs?
Oh, oh.

That is true. The
Minister of Agriculture will bear me out. He knows, because he has been written to about the matter. In the class B fair, there is class 1 and class 2. It has been suggested to him, as the hon. member for Kindersley points out, that the class 2-B fair, should receive the same consideration as the class 1-B fair. The four that are receiving the grant have, I think, been accepted as class 2-B fairs. The 1-B class practically controls the B class fair, and they have not seen fit to allow the new B class fair to get into the 1-B class and they propose to segregate them as 2-B class fairs. What the hon. member for Kindersley states is absolutely correct. In my home town we have the same condition as he describes. The minister has been approached regarding this matter by those that are looking for this assistance, and I should like the minister, through the Minister of Finance, to state what position these 2-B class fairs are in.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I assume hon. members
will present in writing to the minister their statements with respect to the qualifications to share in the grant in question. The only difficulty that I had about the matter was in ascertaining just why four should suddenly become entitled to a grant by telegram during the election, but that may have been due to an oversight. Presumably the matter became so pressing because it had been overlooked, as much departmental business necessarily is, and it was taken care of in that way. May I observe in all these matters no new policy has been initiated by the Minister of Agriculture. If hon. members will take the trouble to look at the supplementary estimates presented on May 11, 1922, by the then government with respect to the previous fiscal year, they will find that the late Mr. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, took complete control of the estimates. They will find on column 1662 of Hansard how he dealt with them and got them passed. I am bound to say that no such information was given then as has been given on this occasion.

Neither the Hon. Mr. Fielding nor the succeeding Minister of Finance took the responsibility of answering for every department. The ministers were in their places and ready to answer if questions were asked.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That may be, but all
the answers were given by the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding.

I was
present in the House of Commons at the time and have been on every occasion since, and the ministers always answered the questions that were asked. The Minister of Finance of course took charge.
Mr. MeINTOSH:	Might I suggest to the
Prime Minister in connection with his agricultural policy that it may be wise to launch a new policy with regard to these fairs? There are two class B fairs: 1-B and 2-B. I do not know what grants the government is going to give to class 2-B fairs, but I know what grant has been given to the class 1-B fair, and that is $1,500 a year. The class A fair has been receiving $5,000 a year. Regina gets $5,000; Saskatoon gets $5,000, and other fairs are getting $5,000-fairs which in my estimation are not doing as good work for agriculture as those in many of the smaller cities like Yorkton, Prince Albert, North Battleford and so forth. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that when he is investigating policies with regard to agricultural fairs he endeavour to remove that grievance. The class 1-B fair ought perhaps to be put into the same category as class A, and given the same grant, namely, $5,000 a year.

Every year during the past several years we members from the west, when the grants to class B fairs came up for discussion, have urged that something should
Supply-Agriculture

be done about them. These grants to class B fairs were started several years ago under the Union government to promote agriculture, more especially in the outlying districts. A closed list was formed, and if you happened to have a fair of a certain size, you got the grant; and if your fair was not up to that size, you did not get the grant. We contended year after year in this house that there should be some policy laid down with respect to these class B fairs, and urged that any fair coming up to a certain standard should get the grant. I make that same recommendation to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) now, that he decide upon a standard for the class B fairs, and that any fair coming up to that standard get the grant; if the fairs now getting the grant do not come up to that standard, withhold the grant. Assiniiboia gets a grant for a class B fair. When these grants were first inaugurated, that was a new country, hardly settled, but it has now a bigger fair than many other towns of larger size. We always contended that we were absolutely entitled to the grant and that we should not be discriminated against just because ours was a young fair, and finally we got the grant. I would again urge the minister to establish a standard for these fairs and that every fair coming up to that standard should get the grant.

The information that

These increases were due to an unusual demand for potato inspection for certified seed production in Quebec and Prince Edward Island. As a result of an increase in inspections, there was an increase in the cost of the operation of laboratories and field equipment. The number of plants coming into the country that had to be inspected at ports of entry increased by over nine million. Further, some extensions and improvements were necessary in two or three of the plant pathalogical laboratories. The estimated cost in Prince Edward Island for potato inspection was $30,000, and the actual cost $37,000. The contemplated expenditure in Quebec was $20,000, and the actual expenditure $31,000. The increased cost of laboratory equipment accounted for $2,000.

Before dinner recess I drew attention to the extreme severity of the cutworm outbreak in the west. I have here a map that was sent out by the entomological branch of the Department of Agriculture, a very efficient branch. I should like to know what success they have met with in attacking this invasion of cutworm on the prairie We would like to know if experiments have been made to show how the cutworm larvae have wintered. We are in hopes that a large number of these larvae will have been destroyed by the intermittent freezing and thawing during the last winter. If some accurate information were given out as to the fertile or non-fertile present condition of these larvae, the farmers would be guided as to their spring sowing. They are advised in this bulletin not to sow their grain until small seeding tests have been made and if on May 15 it is found that there is no cutworm, they may sow their fields. That is too late, however; they will run into danger of frost if they wait until May 15 to sow their wheat. I suggest that the minister take steps to test the topsoil where the larvae are located, incubate them and find out the condition of the eggs. If the eggs are found to be in a dormant and non-fertile condition the farmers may feel easy; if on the other hand the eggs are fertile notwithstanding the exposed winter through absence of snow, the farmers might be disposed to follow the advice given by this bulletin. I can assure my hon. friends opposite, however, that the advice given in this bulletin would mean that wheat sown after May 15 would be too late for many districts. I suggest again that experiments be made by testing the incubatory capacity of the larvae, in the same way as hen eggs are tested in an incubator. A test could be made so as to ascertain the percentage of fertile larvae which develop into cutworms and from that stage into the moths. If this procedure is adopted the results would be of great value to the farmers in determining the date of their spring sowing, because if eggs prove non-fertile, seeding can proceed forthwith as soon as spring opens.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member is aware of the fact that the Department of Agriculture works in conjunction with the provincial departments of agriculture in these matters. At this moment field studies are being carried on for the very purposes mentioned by my hon. friend. Necessarily in a country as large as this those studies must be of local import and are carried on largely through the efforts of the provincial authorities with the aid of skilled and scientific assistants which may be furnished by the federal Department of Agri-

culture. That work is being carried on, and a brochure is now in process of being printed which will contain the information gathered through the efforts of these provincial and federal authorities. It is believed that the knowledge thus obtained from actual field studies will enable the farmer to be advised as to how best to cope with the evil the hon. gentleman has so properly mentioned.

Item agreed to.
Welland ship canal; construction and betterment-further amount required, $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend asked for some information as to the last payments made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: Yes, in connection with the Welland canal. J. P. Porter received his last payment on December 12, 1930; Lyall and Sons, on November 13, 1930; J. P. W. Robertson on November 13. In connection with the powerhouse substructure the last payment is on September 16 made to Messrs. Aiken, Inness & MacLachlan and McLachan. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That exhausted those payments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
So that we may understand the significance to be attached to the main estimates when they are brought down, I wish to ask my right hon. friend if the procedure attempted and being countenanced to-day will be followed by the administration in the next fiscal year. If for example, parliament is asked to appropriate $7,000,000 for the Welland canal in the main estimates, are we to assume that that $7,000,000 is the total amount to be spent within the next fiscal year, or will the total amount to be spent be $9,000,000 or $10,000,000, made so by orders in council passed in 
order to enable the contractor to continue the work? The reference to the estimates made by my right hon. friend means something or nothing, and I would like to have an explanation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend in .making his observations has done some violence to his own equipment. It must be perfecty obvious that unless there is a contract outstanding there can be no expenditures, and the contractor has the option to finish his work within the time stipulated by his contract. We on the other hand have the option of not paying until there has been a further appropriation. We are bound however for the work done within the terms of the contract. Failure to do so constitutes a breach of contract. Therefore parliament must provide or take the consequences of the breach of contract. That is all that is involved in these payments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend must realize that this is not a new contract.
That has nothing to do with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If one could attach any value to what my hon. friend has muttered one certainly would not attach much importance to it as a matter of law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I did not mutter anything.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, my right hon. friend did not; it was an hon. member. Clause 43 reads as follows:
Should the amount voted by parliament and applicable towards payment for the works hereby contracted for, be at any time expended previous to the completion of the works, the minister or the engineer may give the contractor written notice to that effect. Upon receiving such notice the contractor may, if he thinks fit, stop the work-but shall not be entitled to any payment for work done beyond the amount voted and applicable, as aforesaid -until the necessary funds shall have been voted by parliament in that behalf. And in no event shall the contractor have or make any claim on His Majesty for any damages or compensation by reason of the suspension of payment, or by reason of any delay or loss caused by the stoppage of the work. And in the event of the contractor electing to proceed, or proceeding with such work after such notice-
Such notice was given in this case.

and before suoh additional funds are voted, no action of the engineer, or of any other person on behalf of His Majesty, in giving orders, instructions, or directions, or otherwise

Supply-Welland Canal
acting with respect to such work, shall be taken or considered as in any manner improving the rights of the contractor or as waiving in any particular any of the provisions of this section.
In other words this whole contract contemplated the possibility of a contractor being ahead of the appropriations when doing his work, and such contractor took the chances. Further, in five cases out of every ten in this country a similar practice is followed. I could go further and say that it is followed in 75 per cent of the cases. The minister might expect that $25,000 would be sufficient for a particular year but he might spend $100,000. The next year the same thing might happen.

My right
hon. friend knows better than that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I know just that, and
there is one instance in Edmonton at this very time.
But my right hon. friend knows that appropriations are made on the recommendation of engineers of the department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I know how they are cut down. The engineer may recommend $100,000 but the Prime Minister may cut it down to $50,000 and say that that is sufficient.
Quite right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but that does not
interfere with the validity of the contract and the necessity of paying the contract price. That is the procedure in most contracts. The complaint made by my hon. friend's leader i3 that the present practice is so unusual and so unheard of that the whole fabric of government is threatened and all the institutions of this country may be swept away. As a matter of fact what is being done in this case has been done in three-quarters of all the cases in this country. In all the cases I read this afternoon in connection with orders in council which were signed in July these conditions prevailed and they will continue to prevail where there is a time limit for the conclusion of the contract. The contractor takes the chance when he goes forward with his work that there will be a vote from parliament.
He waits for the appropriation; he does not get it the way my right hon. friend is giving it to him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Is there ever a time
when there is justification for the payment of the bill?

Only when his contract is
finished, if he takes upon himself the responsibility of going ahead with the work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The clause I read provides that the contractor will get his money but in the meantime he must spend his own.

That clause provides also
that there is no possibility for payment on the part of the government unless money is voted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Unless it is voted, of course not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: All that my right hon. friend has read only goes to confirm the contention which we who sit on this side have made, namely that the contractor has no claim against the country for any work for which there has not been special provision made by parliament. That is the essence of the clause which my right hon. friend has read.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, just the opposite.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No matter v.hat work he proceeds with, unless parliament has made the appropriation for that work he is not entitled to any claim whatever and, as I say, it simply confirms the statement that the ministry in this action has been taking an entirely wrong course.
Now may I come back to the Welland canal. That contract has been continuing for many years; I think it runs back ten years or more. This house has been voting a certain sum year after year for a certain amount of work to be done. I do not recall any previous year in which any of the contractors on the Welland canal ventured to go beyond the amount of work for which this parliament voted money, but this year, when parliament has appropriated $7,000,000 my hon. friends, after they come into office, say to the contractors, "Parliament has voted only $7,000,000, but you are at liberty to go ahead and incur an expenditure of $9,000,000. We have a majority in the house and we will see that you get your extra $2,000,000, if you wait until parliament reassembles." What I want to ask my right hon. friend is this: If that is the proper and legal way of proceeding this year it will be equally proper and legal next year, and if my right hon. friend comes to parliament with his estimates after the Easter recess and there is an amount included therein of $7,000,000 for the Welland canal, what guarantee has this house that this amount of $7,000,000 will represent what the government proposes to spend on the Welland canal next year? If they follow the course they are adopting now it will not be $7,000,000; it will be $9,000,000. If we allow this

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Supply-Welland Canal

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: matter to pass and this action on the part of the ministry to become a precedent there is no reason why it should not be $10,000,000 or $11,000,000. In other words the whole principle involved in the appropriating of public moneys by vote of parliament is of no value; it becomes null and void. I say, Mr. Chairman, this is wholly irregular. I cannot understand what my right hon. friend can have in mind when in one breath he talks about the necessity of reforming the financial methods of the country, and the next moment comes before parliament and asks us to make an appropriation of $2,000,000 for work which already has been performed under order in council and not in any particular by authority of parliament.
Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman; I cannot let the erroneous statements remain without making a proper explanation. Once more I say to the right hon. gentleman that he does not seem to appreciate or understand the value of a contract. According to his statement all you would have to do would be to let the contractor go ahead and finish his work and then find no money for him, and he could not get it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would not allow him to go ahead; I would have him stop when the money was used up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: You cannot make him stop, because you have entered into exactly the opposite kind of contract.

What was
the meaning of what my right hon. friend read a moment ago?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That provides for this
very case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Read it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will read it again:
Should the amount voted by parliament and applicable towards payment for the works hereby contracted for, be at any time expended previous to the completion of the works, the minister or the engineer may give the contractor written notice to that effect.
Any one who is familiar with the interpretation of contracts knows that this merely means that when the appropriation is exhausted, the contractor is so advised. Then it proceeds:
Upon receiving such notice, the contractor may, if he thinks fit, stop the work,-but shall not be entitled to any payment for work done beyond the amount voted and applicable, as aforesaid-until the necessary funds shall have been voted by parliament in that behalf.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What does that mean?
No liability until parliament votes the money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly; the liability
is there, but there is no claim. May I say to those hon. gentlemen who happen to be lawyers that in the Windsor v. Annapolis railway case the authority is contained for what I have said. If that is not sufficient authority, there is the case of Onderdonk v. the King. The third case is McEwen v. the King and the next is the case of Creelman v. the King. I happen to know about these cases because I had something to do with two of them. This paragraph which I have read merely provides that upon receiving such notice, the contractor may, if he thinks fit, stop his work. If he stops, then well and good, but he cannot stop; he must go ahead to complete the work within the time limit.

He does not have to go
ahead if he is notified to stop.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, that is not what he is notified. If in a court of law counsel made a statement like that I know what the .judge would say. He is told that he will have to wait for his money until parliament provides it, and that is all. All that is suggested from the other side is this: never provide him with that money and never pay for the work. In other words we are told that we should repudiate the contract by not appropriating money. Do hon. gentlemen opposite mean to say that any contractor could not get a fiat for that?
You do not repudiate the contract if you act according to its terms.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But you do not act
according to the terms of it.

If my right hon. friend will permit me to finish, I was going to say that the contract contemplates the giving of notice and the stopping of work, and the fact that the contractor shall not be entitled to his money unless that money has been voted by parliament. He therefore does take the risk, but he knows he takes the risk when he enters into the contract. Therefore there is no repudiation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend
realizes what it says: it says he may stop work if he thinks fit. If he goes on-
He takes the risk.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The risk of what?

The risk of the vote never being made.

Supply-Welland, Canal

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I had some little respect for my hon. friend's legal ability, but surely he does not mean that.
I say that is the risk he takes, the risk of the money never being voted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The risk of parliament
never voting the money?
Yes.
It is the risk the Postmaster General takes-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think junior counsel
will add nothing to the argument. May I venture to say that my hon. friend from Shel-burne-Yarmouth will remember the old maxim, "the infallible justice of the crown." The crown cannot repudiate a contract by failing to do what parliament is bound to do, having entered into a contract for a party to finish work within a fixed time, and not having voted enough money to finish it within the first year, or within the term fixed for its completion, if the contractor goes ahead and does it at this risk, the risk being that parliament must vote the money. The crown cannot escape its responsibility by failing to discharge the obligation imposed upon it by this contract, the obligation being to pay the amount required. That condition does not relieve the crown from paying.
The contract says he is not to be paid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, quite the opposite.
Then what was the object of the order in council?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not read the clause which states that a definite time has been fixed within which this work is to be completed. That is the vital point in his present argument. In that connection may I remind him of what the minister in charge of this department has said. The minister told us that this additional work was gone on with in order to furnish work for the unemployed. The twTo statements do not hold together. The minister on the one hand says: "We spent $2,000,000 additional on the Welland canal because there were men unemployed this winter, and the government thought this was a good way to give them employment." The Prime Minister now says this $2,000,000 is required because the contract has to be completed within a specified time and it has not been so completed. I say that either one of these explanations is the correct one and the other is incorrect, or maybe both 22110-28J
of them are incorrect. The point I should like my right hon. friend to clear up now is where in the contract the clause is which states that this work must be completed within a certain time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid few things better illustrate the attitude of mind of the right hon. gentleman that what he has just said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Never mind my attitude of mind; let us have the facts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Do not get excited;
possess thy soul in patience. The illustration I had in mind with respect to a contract in which a certain time was named was given this afternoon-I had the date before me, July 30, 1930. That was the contract for the central heating in this city, and that is the case to which I referred.- I had not the papers with respect to the Welland canal. I was illustrating my point and I did not say there was a definite date or that this work was done for that purpose. I said, "assume that the contractor desires to do it." Last fall, on September 7, in this house, in the remarks I then made, I pointed out that if favouring conditions made it possible the government would, on a unit basis, proceed with the work if it added no extra cost, for the purpose of providing employment to people in a given area, and I took Port Arthur by way of illustration. This, as a matter of fact, affords a second illustration, and as it happened, at the unit cost the contractor went on with his work and gave employment, to a thousand people in one instance, and several hundred in another. I cannot see that anything I have said detracts from the general principle that, in the extraordinary circumstances that arose in connection with the unemployment situation, which was a national problem, where a unit cost was fixed for the construction of works under an outstanding contract, and it was within the time fixed for the completion, if the work were expedited by the contractor for the purpose of supplying employment to a large number of people it was a perfectly legal and proper exercise of power to allow the continuance of operations. And upon parliament devolves the legal obligation, the infallible justice of the crown, at the first moment that the house meets afterwards, to supply the contractor with the money to compensate him for the work he has done. I do not think there is any doubt as to that being the practice followed in this country from time immemorial, and it will be the practice in the future. Wherever work is done within the time fixed for the completion of the contract and the contractor goes forward, takes
Supply-Welland Canal

his chance and does his work, the crown is bound at the first session to provide the money he has expended to prevent him from going into bankruptcy, as one contractor did because of the failure of the crown to supply him with the money he had expended.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We now have a third reason for the expenditure. My right hon. friend says that parliament should make provision in this way in order to prevent a contractor from going into bankruptcy.
He did not say that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of course he i id it; they were the last words he used before he sat down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not this contractor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not this contractor, no. We have had three separate explanations. One is that the contractor may go into bankruptcy-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen are not anxious to have the estimates passed they may proceed as they wish. These are not our estimates; I wish to make that clear. The late Liberal administration when in office presented certain estimates to the house in the form of main estimates. They were carefully reviewed before parliament prorogued and a supplementary estimate was brought down. Hon. gentlemen opposite were then on this side and they were free to criticize the estimates. We made the statement that according to our best study-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There was no criticism
of this item.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
-what we were asking for was all that we considered necessary. With respect to the Welland canal, which is only one case in point, we asked for an expenditure of $7,000,000 for the fiscal year. That was the extent of our estimate. Now we are confronted with a supplementary estimate for $2,000,000 for the Welland canal in addition to the $7,000,000 which we said was sufficient and all that should have been expended in the last fiscal year having regard to what was being spent on other public works in other parts of the Dominion. The question which many hon. members opposite as well as members on this side are asking themselves is this: Why should the contractors on the Welland canal and up at Fort William and Port Arthur be specially favoured in one case to the extent of an additional appropriation of $2,000,000 and in the other of a quarter of a million dollars, while the contractors in

other parts of the Dominion receive nothing additional and even in some cases, where we had unemployed walking the streets and parliament had made an appropriation for buildings, contractors should receive no authority even to proceed with work for which parliament had made appropriations. The excuses and circumlocutions of my right hon. friend up to the present are not adequate to satisfy us on this side of the house as to the wisdom of voting this amount at this time. I want to get from my right hon. friend before this item is passed the clause in the contract which provides that the work must be completed within a period of time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then I wish
him to say that there was not such a clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said I did not know.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We will wait
until my right hon. friend gets the information. We are entitled to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?
No.
Carried.
Stands.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This house is entitled to the information. Last session we voted $20,000,000 without question for unemployment relief and now we are told that there is in connection with the Welland canal $2,000,000 spent in addition, according to the minister, for the relief of unemployment. The Prime Minister gave the explanation that it was because of some legal requirement which obliged him to see that the contractor was paid if the work was done within a certain time. And he said that no contractor should go into bankruptcy. This country is entitled to know the terms of the contract in its entirety and on what grounds we are asked to vote this extra $2,000,000. I therefore ask the Prime Minister or the minister to give the house the terms of the contract with respect to the matter, indicating the time limit within which the work should be done, together with a copy of the order in council which was passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is within the right of hon. gentlemen if they desire to delay this estimate, and I wish them much joy in so doing. I think this country will properly appraise their value. The truth is that these men have spent this money, they have done the work. The reasons moving towards the

Supply-Welland Canal
doing of the work are matters of record. It helped unemployment and enabled them to keep their crew together. The freeze-up was later than usual and the fall was open. Not a single cent more has been expended on this work by the country on this account, and the leader of the opposition, who at one time led a government, comes into the house and tries first to raise the sectional issue. He says, "How is it that this much has been spent here and not elsewhere?" That is the sectional issue. Year after year millions of dollars have been voted in connection with the Welland canal, which is a link in a great chain of transportation. This is a very ambitious undertaking on the part of a population of less than ten millions and at a cost of $100,000,000 or more; and it will cost probably $125,000,000 or more before completion. When the minister said that the work was gone on with because it would furnish employment, that was perfectly correct; and 1 pointed out, as I repeat now, that this item is in the estimates because it represents toil, labour, material furnished by the contractors under the contracts-because there are many contracts, as the house knows, covering various sections of the canal. I say, therefore, that the contractors are entitled, at the first session of parliament after the work has been done, to the provision of the money necessary to compensate them for the services which they have rendered. This must be done or parliament ceases to keep faith with its own contractors.
Now, I said this afternoon that there was an order in council with respect to the matter. The minister tells me that no order in council was passed. No authorization by order in council was required for the work to be proceeded with and none was passed. They merely went ahead with the work, because there was no limitation imposed upon them to stop. They went ahead knowing that the appropriation had not been made, but they took their chance. The illustration I gave, happened to have reference to the Welland canal. Hon. gentlemen know that it is an old device to endeavour to divert an illustration to a particular case before the house. As a matter of fact, no such effort was made on my part, for I had no figures indicating when the contract was to be completed. It may have been that it should be completed years hence or when all the work was done. I did not know; I was not concerned about it. But I did give an illustration, one in which the Public Works department provided a date within which the work was to be completed.
I showed that on July 26 last an order in council had been passed by the late administration. I did not for a moment suggest that it was passed improperly-in my judgment it was properly passed-because if business is to be carried on in a proper and legitimate manner work should be done without adding any cost to the public or increasing by a single cent the money that must be paid for the service rendered. This is especially so in cases where the work will give employment to several thousand people at a time when employment is at a premium. At such times it is not the privilege but the duty of a government to afford a contractor the opportunity to do the work. When, as in this case, the contractors signified their willingness to take the risk in the good faith of parliament, then I submit that it is only a proper exercise of its power that parliament should grant supply for that purpose. If this committee desires further information and asks for the production of contracts which might be brought before it when the general estimates are under consideration, that procedure will have to be followed. If it is desired to hold up this estimate for the Welland canal until to-morrow, it is always within the power of the opposition to do so. Whether or not that power is properly exercised is not for me to say; that is for them to determine. The general estimates will afford an opportunity to consider this matter in its entirety, as well as every matter which we have been discussing. Of course the identical items will not be before the committee, but so far as any discussion upon the principle of appropriation and expenditure is concerned, the general estimates will provided a most ample opportunity to secure from the ministers in charge of the respective departments such information as is desired. I submit that it has never been the custom for the house to pursue the course which my hon. friend suggests should be pursued in this case. Notwithstanding what the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) has said, the discussion on similar estimates in the past does not seem to have been carried on by any minister other than the Minister of Finance. They were passed very rapidly in bulk, and that seemed to be the end of them. I did think at that time, and I still think I was right in suggesting, that the widest possible explanation be given in the estimates themselves so that the members of the committee might have before them such reasonable details as it was possible to give as to how the moneys were to be made up. When the former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) inquired as to this matter, I thought reasonable explanation should be
Supply-Welland Canal

forthcoming with respect to this item, as to how much each contractor earned as certified by those who checked their work. This is merely an effort to relieve them in respect of the liabilities neoessarily incurred in carrying on work of this kind, and also to keep the good faith of the country with the contractors.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My right hon. friend has referred to the opposition as having certain powers. May I remind him that the opposition has also certain duties, and the first duty of an opposition is-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: To oppose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
-to safeguard public expenditures; to see that the moneys of the people are expended in accordance with the methods provided by the constitution, and that the requirements of the law and the practices of parliament in all particulars are fully carried out. In view of the latest explanations which have been given, the situation seems to be going from bad to worse. The Prime Minister admitted this afternoon that no appropriation had been made by parliament for this purpose, and we assumed naturally that in that event there had been a governor general's warrant. My right hon. friend then said that no warrant had been issued, and we began to consider how these contractors came to have the right to receive $2,000,000 from the public treasury for expenditures incurred in connection with the construction of the canal. We assumed that the government as a whole had some responsibility in the matter, and I asked my right hon. friend how that responsibility had been assumed. I received from him the reply that an order in council had been passed. He now tells us that no order in council was passed. If we had left the matter where it was this afternoon, where my right hon. friend thought we ought to leave it in order to save time, the record would have been to the effect that an order in council had been passed and the public would have assumed that the members of the government, who have a collective responsibility, had known something of this transaction. I submit that parliament and the country have a right to assume that the Prime Minister would be very careful in making a statement of that kind. The right hon. gentleman found fault with me because I complained-I complained in the interests of the country-of his taking upon his shoulders all the work of government. If there ever was a reason why each minister of the crown should explain his own estimates, we have it in the remarks of the Prime Minister this

afternoon when he, as president of the council and the one who signs the orders, told the country that an order in council had been passed authorizing this expenditure, and then comes back in the evening, after further consultation with the minister of the department, and tells us that no order was passed. What are we now reduced to by way of authority for expenditure of this $2,000,000? It has come down to the mere word of a minister. In other words, the precedent being established at this time is that under the present administration-this is the first opportunity we have had to question them on their methods-all that any contractor who has a contract for any given amount appropriated by this parliament needs to do in order to go ahead after that amount has been fully expended, is to have the direction of the minister in charge of the department to go ahead; then parliament will be asked to vote the money and because the government has a majority he will receive it in due course. My colleague to my right tells me that he does not even need that, and when I reflect upon the Prime Minister's words I am inclined to think that he is correct. From what the Prime Minister told us, all the contractor has to do is just go ahead and spend as much money as he likes and then it will be up to the infallible justice of the crown-to use the phrase that was used-to see that the amounts are paid. If that is the way in which public moneys are to be appropriated by this administration, the sooner we understand it the better, because it is altogether contrary to the proper method and it should not be sanctioned for one moment.
I have no desire to delay my hon. friend in getting his estimates through, and I think I have done as much as any one in this parliament to facilitate the passing of estimates. However, I am going to see to it that in attempting as I shall to facilitate the business of the house we receive the information to which we are entitled and that nothing is going to be put over by mere bluff.
Order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We are going
to ascertain the facts and we are going to understand them.
I would ask my right hon. friend to let us have this contract and a statement of the expenditures which have been made under it so that we may consider it. In the meantime, the item might stand over until to-morrow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was my impression
that an order had been passed. Upon inquiry, I found that although preparation had been

Supply-Welland Canal
made for an order in council the legal advisers of the department were of the opinion that it was unnecessary. Whereupon the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals wrote to each contractor, in the following words:
It is the desire of the Department of Railways and Canals that the construction of the said works be continued, without suspension thereof, pending the voting by parliament of the necessary funds therefor, and, in the event of your electing under the provisions of clause 43 aforesaid to so continue the construction of the said works, I have to assure you that early in the coming session parliament will be asked to vote an additional amount to make payment under the said contract for the construction of the works so continued.
That was signed by the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals.
Addressed to whom?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Addressed to each of the contractors.

That
makes it worse than ever.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That letter was dated
December 27, 1930. The contractors had represented that owing to the conditions then existing they could continue the work without cessation at the same unit price, supply some employment to the unemployed, and carry forward their undertaking. That is the contract which has always existed with reference to that work; there was no change. I regret having made the statement that an order in council had been passed. The question was asked and I answered as I did knowing that the material for an order in council had been prepared by the minister. I recalled later that the legal opinion was that it was unnecessary to have an order in council. The terms of the contract were such that it was sufficient that a notice be given by the deputy miinster, and the letter I have just read contains the terms under which they continued their work.
I would be the last person in the world to suggest that an opposition should fail in its duty, but I find it difficult to understand just what is involved in the production of a dozen contracts that I have not seen, that were made, as the right hon. gentleman said, at least ten years ago, and that are still in force and effect and will be for some time. I am not conscious of endeavouring to withhold from the committee any information and I think I have given it somewhat fuller information than ever before has been placed upon the records in connection with supplementary estimates, not for a further year but with respect to a period that has passed. I think in previous years you will look in vain for details with respect to similar estimates.

Was the letter which has
just been read written at the request of the contractor?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was written after the contractor and the deputy minister had had a conference, in order to regularize a matter having regard to section 43 of the contract, which section I read a few minutes ago.

Does that not put a different interpretation on the matter from the one the right hon. gentleman has given? We find now that a new contract has been entered into between the Department of Railways and the contractor; or rather, it is not a new contract but they have authorized an obligation binding upon the so-called infallible justice of the crown, because it is a written contract. As the Prime Minister explained his position to us, he stated that under the old contract as he read it to the committee, the crown was bound to make payments for this work provided that the contractor decided to carry on, and this was at the contractor's option. Now we find from the letter which the Prime Minister has read that these contractors, as a result of conference with the deputy minister, exacted from the deputy minister a letter regularizing their position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps it would help
the matter if the hon. gentleman had the other part of the letter. I was directing myself entirely to one portion of it.

If the hon. gentleman will
not put all the facts before us, how are we to judge?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The other part shows
the contract that was referred to. I did not think it necessary to read it, and I do not think my hon. friend would have done so had he been in my place. It is as follows:
In accordance with the provisions of clause 43 of your contract No. 24275, dated the 18th day of August, 1921, entered into with His Majesty the King, therein represented by the Minister of Railways and Canals, for the construction and completion of sections Nos. 1 and 2 of the Welland Ship canal, I hereby give you notice that the amount voted by parliament and applicable towards payment for the works thereby contracted for has been expended.
Then came the second part which is exactly within the terms of section 43.
Supply-Welland Canal
No. The second one is not within the terms of section 43.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The second paragraph
quotes it.

Does the paragraph not suggest that the contractors go on with the work and promise to get a vote of parliament? What the minister is doing is asking parliament to make good this letter written by the deputy minister.
Mr. Chairman-
Another legal mind.

No it is not a legal mind. Perhaps it is just as well for the lawyers to let the rest of us have an opportunity to discuss the matter. Am I right in assuming that the Deputy Minister of Railways wrote that letter to the contractor on the advice and instruction of the minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
If the letter had not been sent, would that money have been due to the contractors, according to the contract?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, the money would still be due without the letter.
Were there accounts still pending?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there are large accounts pending and the country would still be liable. The contractor chose to go on.
I would ask the Prime Minister to produce the letter and give the date of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did. It is dated 23rd December, 1030.
I understand a large part of the $2,000,000 was already spent at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: None of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not at that time. I gave the date of the last payment in answer to a question of the leader of the opposition.
That is not the date the work was done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The work was done subsequently to that and the amount of work done by Porter came to $40,000, that done by Peter Lyall and Sons to $203,000, and so on, making a little over $2,000,000.
Would the hon. gentleman put on Hansard the names of those who are to profit by this $2,000,000?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I gave them to Hansard a moment or two ago in answer to my right hon. friend.

It seems to me that this is a most extraordinary situation. As I understand it-and I trust the Prime Minister, or his deputy, the Minister of Railways and Canals, will correct me if I am wrong-last year at the regular session parliament voted the sum of $7,000,000 for the Welland canal. I understand there is on record a letter from the deputy minister to the contractor, advising him that that amount of money was exhausted, that is, the amount legally and properly voted by last year's parliament. I further understand that the Prime Minister, in explaining the matter to parliament to-day, said that in speaking of the $20,000,000 voted last year at the special session for unemployment relief, he referred to certain possible undertakings, including perhaps the undertaking which we are now discussing, which might have to be resorted to by the government in order to relieve unemployment throughout Canada. If this amount of $2,000,000 had been (taken out of the unemployment relief fund regularly voted by parliament, I would raise no objection whatsoever. But the point is this: it is much worse than proceeding by order in council. Here you have a contractor or a number of contractors carrying on public undertakings in the Dominion of Canada on the signed letter of a deputy minister of the crown without ever having received the authority of parliament. That is the situation and I suggest to the Prime Minister that these contractors financed their undertakings from the banks on the authority of a letter from the deputy minister, which letter has been produced by the Prime Minister. Therefore we are in the position to-day that a letter from a permanent official of the crown is supplementing the regular authority of parliament when a vote becomes a grant. During the special session of parliament, the Prime Minister took away from parliament its power over taxation. He is now taking away from parliament its control over public contracts throughout the Dominion.
Mr. CASGRAiIN: Do I understand that two letters were written by the deputy minister to the contractor, one stating that the amount of money appropriated was exhausted, and the other advising the various

Supply-Welland Canal
contractors that they could go on with their work and be paid afterwards by amounts of money that would be voted by parliament? If there are two such letters, I ask the government to produce them.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There was just one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said there was only one, and I read it.
Both statements, I understand, were in the same letter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

In view of the anxiety regarding unemployment, may I ask the Prime Minister whether the policy followed in connection with the Welland canal was the policy followed by this government after July 28 last, in connection with other government contracts?

The Prime Minister has, of course, taken the leadership with regard to the supplementary estimates, but every minister of the government of which I was a member used to be instructed to be iri his place in the house and to be prepared to answer any question which might arise in respect to his department.
