It has taken a long time to produce this letter, but we know now that this government is irrevocably committed to paying this two million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: So was your government.
Not necessarily. I beg to differ.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The contract was there.

The contract was there, I admit, but parliament up to a recent date had authority even over contracts. If the situation is to be changed, we had better know it. If the government of the day and contractors are to be all-powerful and to supersede parliament, the sooner we know it the better. But the government of which I was a member did not proceed in that way. I do not suggest that governments can repudiate contracts, but it surely would be a pice thing to have a progressive contract punning over two or three years and parliament having no control over the expenditure until the work was done.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We have control. We
pre dealing with the matter now.

I beg to
differ. Year after year estimates were brought down for the Welland canal and voted by parliament. The expenditures were made under those estimates, and when the estimates ceased, the work ceased. That has been the
system pursued with respect to work on the Welland canal. I am willing to admit that fast year was an exceptional year, and if our hon. friends opposite had told us that this work was undertaken for the purpose of giving employment, and if the letter binding the government had been produced, I do not think the government would have had as much trouble as they are having this evening over this particular item.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The hon.
member for Northumberland has asked a question to which I think he is entitled to an answer. I confess that we are still a little in doubt as to what the attitude or policy of .the government is in this matter. As I said a moment ago, the Prime Minister has indicated that in some way or another it related to the time factor and to legal conditions of the contract, but I am prepared to take the .word of the minister of the department, who .was of the view which the Prime Minister subsequently veered round to, that this work was in part gone on with because of the unemployment conditions existing. I shall not inquire too far, but will say that apparently such was the policy, to provide work for the relief of unemployment. The question which the hon. member for Northumberland has Risked is whether that policy was adopted with respect to other works in Canada or whether it was confined to work on the Welland canal. If that was the policy, and it applied to other works, what were the other works to which it applied? I think we are entitled to an answer to that question.

As a member representing largely a labour riding I am very pleased indeed at the attitude of the opposition tonight on this question. The leader of the opposition has just stated that in his opinion the government did this work to relieve unemployment, and yet we find him and his own party condemning the government for having spent two million dollars to help relieve the unemployment situation in this country.
We are not condemning the government. We are asking for information.

You are camouflaging. For hours this evening the party opposite has been condemning the government for spending this two million dollars, and it was not two million dollars of their own money. The contractors spent the money, and it did not cost the Dominion government one extra dollar. The party opposite has objected to paying the contractors for the money they spent on that work. That is the situation we find
Supply-Welland Canal

in this house to-night, and as a member representing to a large extent a labouring constituency I am glad that the opposition have made their attitude known.
May I ask if the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario was speaking for the Prime Minister or for the Minister of Railways?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know how carefully the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has been following the discussion, but certainly he has heard no word from my lips condemning any assistance given to relieve unemployment. What I have been trying to ascertain, and am still trying to ascertain from the government, is whether this work was undertaken for the purpose of relieving unemployment. If that was part of the government's policy, I am asking whether that policy was confined to the work on the Welland canal or extended to other public works in this country; and if so, what those public works were. I am asking for that information and would like my right hon. friend to give an answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did state to the committee this afternoon that the government had taken the estimates prepared by hon. gentlemen opposite, and so far as was reasonably possible, where the situation warranted it, the government called for tenders and carried on contracts for the purpose of supplying the public works required; and especially was that so where by so doing employment would be furnished to anyone. That is what was done. If hon. gentlemen, when the main estimates are before the house, will take the estimates of last year and compare them with the expenditures made during the year, with the contracts outstanding and the sums of money that it will be essential to vote in the main estimates to carry to completion the works thus started, I think they will agree that, to a very large degree, a real and earnest effort has been made, to carry out wherever possible undertakings that would not only meet the public demands but help also to supply employment to those who needed it.
I am not satisfied from the evidence I have at hand that the policy referred to by the Prime Minister with regard to the Welland canal was made applicable to other government contracts.
I understood the Prime Minister to say that the committee would be given the benefit of a copy of the order in council. I presume he will bring down also whatever other documents are relevant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said there was no order in council.
I beg pardon-the contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Do not have any misunderstanding. I did not say the contract. I said that the production of it would serve no useful purpose.

If my right hon. friend has not already agreed to that, I do wish to point out that enough has been revealed in this discussion, I think, to show that we cannot be perfectly clear as to what is in the contract or what documents are on file without having them produced.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: You ought to know what is in the contract. You made it ten years ago.
We do not carry the details in our heads.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But you expect other people to do so.

Probably if we had been as close to it as my right hon. friend we would have remembered whether there was any time limit, which is, I understand, one of the essential points which was suggested by my right hon. friend as constituting a ground for liability. We do not know whether there was a time limit or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not suggest that there was a time limit, because I said that I did not know what was in it.

My right hon. friend was
giving that as a reason generally why there was liability under these contracts and why we had to pay a contractor because, he said, there was a time limit in most of these contracts, and if the contractor did his work on time we were liable to him whether parliament voted the money or not. I understand now that the Prime Minister does not know whether there is a time limit in the contract or not. That can only be decided by an inspection of the contract itself. Secondly, it was thought that there was an order in council extending the time and asking the contractors to go ahead. Apparently that is not correct; there was nothing more than a draft order in council which it was not considered necessary to pass in view of the advice of the iaw officers of the crown. But the remarkable thing that has come out in this discussion is the letter which my right hon. friend has read. The term of the contract is that if the appropriation has run out the government may give notice that the appropriation has

Supply-Welland Canal
expired and then if the contractor goes on he does so at his own risk. Apparently the government wanted the contractor to go on notwithstanding the fact that the appropriation had expired. If they wanted him to go on why did they give notice at all? What is the use of this stop and start notice-and that is all it is-all in the same breath? One minute the government says the appropriation has expired, with the consequences which the contract specifies but, the next minute it says in effect: "Even though there is no appropriation and even though the contract says you go on at your own risk, go ahead; we shall be very glad if you will go on and we will put a vote before parliament at the next session." That is the situation as it appears so far from the documents we have heard, and I feel, as do many other hon. members, that we ought to see the contract and ought to see all the documents just to ascertain the real attitude of the government in regard to the expenditure of this money. It is not a question of criticizing the expenditure if made for the purpose of unemployment; it is a question of the regularity of expenditures and the policy which this government is following in connection with expenditures without previous parliamentary authority. We want to know when we enter into a contract whether the contractor must stop if the money runs out, or if he goes on, does he do so at his own risk. We want to know whether the deputy minister can simply write a letter and do away with the express provision of the contract, and make it absolutely obligatory under the principle of the "infallible justice of the crown" which so often this evening has been invoked that parliament should vote this money. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that you should not press the vote and that your repeated suggestions that the vote "carry" might perhaps be discontinued, if you do not mind. I would suggest that the vote be not carried until the Prime Minister brings down the contract and other documents.
Carried.
May I ask the Prime Minister if it is possible with the documents he has in hand to tell this committee how much of the $2,090,000 was paid as salaries to ordinary working men?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Roughly speaking I
would say in reply there were 2,000 men employed. They were employed during the months of December, January, February and March. The major part of the money expended would be for wages.
The amount is not available?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
On behalf of
the opposition I am asking the Prime Minister to produce the contract under which these moneys are being paid. Do I understand that he refuses to produce the contract?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is the contract
under which the right hon. gentleman has for a period of nine years made payments. It is a contract with which every member of his government is thoroughly familiar. It is not here. It is dated August 18, 1921, and there have been no alterations whatever in it. I refer to one of the Porter contracts; the others may have been on different dates No possible purpose can be served in having it here, and it is not sought for any useful purpose.

Order.
Mr.MACKENZIE KING: The last remark of my right hon. friend is altogether gratuitous and very much out of order. May I say to the Prime Minister that it is quite conceivable that the original contract might contain in it clauses which would prohibit anything in the nature of the action he has taken, and that may be the reason he is trying to keep from this parliament and the country the contract in question. I venture to say my right hon. friend cannot suggest an instance in the history of this parliament where parliament has been asked to vote money under a contract and has been refused the right to see the contract itself. My right hon. friend knows very well that hon. members on this side of the house do not remember the terms of contracts which were passed many years ago. He knows also that no one on this side of the house has attempted to manage the affairs of all the departments of government, or to carry in his mind all the particulars referring to all matters in all departments. We are entitled to the information. I hope the Prime Minister will realize the seriousness of declining to give to this house a contract under which he asks us to vote the sum of $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: So far as I know, Mr. Chairman, there has never been a case in which a contract upon which payments have been made for ten years has been sought by the opposition. Does the right hon. gentleman remember any such contract?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No payments were made by the opposition in this matter.
Supply-Welland Canal

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Did anybody ever hear of such a thing? What relevance has it to this issue? What relevance has it to the payment of $2,000,000 for services rendered and work done?
Why did my right -hon. friend bring down the clause in the contract?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was obtained by one of my hon. friends at dinner time for the purpose of indicating that there was authority to pass the amount.
It is remarkable that we are not entitled to see the other clauses of the contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not the point; the contract is not here and the offices are closed. If it had been, asked for before dinner it would have been here.

Get it to-morrow.
Mr, BENNETT: It may be obtained for to-morrow if the hon. members wish to tie up the estimates. The only question in my mind is whether or not it is right and in the interests of the country to tie up the country's business in this way. This is a contract in connection with which the previous government had knowledge and under which money has been paid for nine years; yet my hon. friends opposite want the people to understand that their solicitude for the public interest is so great that now, on this last day of -the fiscal year, they must -have the contract before payment upon it can be made. My hon. friends talk about their solicitude for the public interest; yet they want to see a contract nine years old. May I ask the exMinister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) who has become so virtuous in his observations in reference to parliamentary institutions and payments from the federal treasury, if he got a governor general's warrant to pay the cost of putting in certain flooring for a political favourite just before the last election? Did he or did he not? Was a governor general's warrant laid upon the table of the house in the early days of the session concerning Mr. Marshall, a former resident of Edmonton and a contractor, giving him money as a gift, by warrant, just before an election?

For doing
what?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: For doing certain work in connection with an elevator in the city of Edmonton.
Amounting to about $25.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not clever.
The Prime Minister says I am not clever.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The Prime
Minister has the floor.
I rise to a point of order. I think the right hon. gentleman has no right to say that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is rising to a point of order he must state the point of order, and the Prime Minister will sit down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What is the point of order?
I would like to know if the right hon. gentleman, who has the reputation of being a one-man government-
Order.
Just a moment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What is the point of order?
I would like to know if he is so much a judge as to reflect on an hon. member of this house in a way that is not parliamentary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member must state his point of order and not make a speech. While I am chairman the rules of the house must be observed, and if hon. members are not satisfied let them appeal to the house.
My point of order, Mr. Chairman, is this: I protest, not because of myself-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not a point of order.

I protest against the term used by the right hon. gentleman, and I ask him to withdraw it, not because of my humble person, but because I am one of the representatives of the people here and he has no right to say that about me. I remember that the right hon. gentleman was called a humbug, and he did not like it, so I do not like him to say that about me. I would like the right hon. gentleman to withdraw that statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member state his point of order?
I would like the right hon. gentleman to withdraw that statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: To withdraw what?
That expression.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
What expression? My hon. friend must understand I cannot hear everything that goes on in this house. If th&

Supply-Welland Canal
hon. member will state which expression he wishes to be withdrawn I will decide on the matter, but I do not know to what expression he has reference. If he does not know himself I cannot guess it.
Of course I do not want to go very far with this matter, Mr. Chairman, but you know very well that this expression is not parliamentary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What expression? If my hon. friend will state it I will be able to give a ruling. If it is not .parliamentary I will ask the right hon. Prime Minister to withdraw it, but the hon. member must state which expression he means.
I am very sorry that the Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I cannot hear everything.
I am very sorry-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will ask the hon. member once more to state his point of order, and if he does not do so I will ask him to take his seat.

If the chairman will allow
me to speak I will state my point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I cannot allow the hon. member to make a speech; he must state his point of order, because he has risen to it.
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, if I were to say that the deputy speaker of the house was not clever, would I have to withdraw that expression?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is that the point of
order my hon. friend is raising? If so, I would not consider it.
Withdraw.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: After these interruptions, Mr. Chairman, I will proceed. I can quite understand, as I said, the solicitude for the public interest which is shown by hon. members opposite, but I find it a little difficult to appreciate in view of the fact that this is a contract under which, according to the statement which was just made, over $7,000,000 was voted last year. It is the same contract with the same people; payment is to be made to them for the same class of services, certified by the same inspectors. The only difference is that they continued their work beyond the appropriation that was made by parliament at the last session.
And that is the difference.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Just what does that involve? Every contract made in this country is open to that construction, and in five cases out of ten that has been done. Looking through the parliamentary proceedings I see no record of any effort to challenge that procedure in respect to contracts sanctioned by parliament. If this contract had not been sanctioned by parliament I could understand it, but under the circumstances hon. members will agree that the time of the house is being needlessly taken up. What will the production of the contract do? What purpose can be served by it? That is the real point. The house has a right to cognizance of the contract. In the main estimates we must vote further moneys for this canal; there are balances still due, and the house once more will determine whether the contract in respect to which the Liberal government voted money for nine years will continue to have money voted under it for two years by a Conservative government. All the hullabaloo has been raised on this point. To quote the language of the right hon. leader of the opposition, is this elevating to the reputation of parliament? Is this calculated to enhance its value in the minds of the public? Is this giving a finer appreciation of the value of parliamentary institutions to those who look on from afar? These are questions which the right hon. gentleman asks so frequently that I may be pardoned if I venture now to make the same inquiry. Apparently the idea is to tie up parliament, to prevent the business from being transacted, because you cannot have brought before you to-night a certain document to which no reference was made before six o'clock. Hon, gentlemen opposite knew the offices would be closed after six, that there would be no opportunity to get the document after that hour, but now they ask that the contract be produced. They gave no notice of such a wish before the dinner adjournment; they indicated no desire of that kind in all the time they had at their disposal. Now, when the vaults are closed and the offices empty, they wish to get the contract in order to delay this item. Well, they can get the delay they desire; I can wait as well as they can wait. I am not in the least worried about it. I hope they will enhance their position before the people of this country, and that my right hon. friend will have the opportunity of referring to the high place that parliamentary institutions must hold in the minds of the people. He should have ample opportunity for making such references, in view of the scenes we have
Supply-Welland Canal

witnessed during the last few minutes. An hon. gentleman opposite rose to a point of order when I remarked about his reference to a governor general's warrant that paid Mr. Robert Marshall something over $25 for work done. I said the hon. gentleman was not clever when he made that reference. Does anyone say he is clever in making an observation of that character? I will leave it at that. Five or ten minutes go by; a whispered consultation is held; the rear troops are brought up; the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) tells the hon. gentleman what he should do in order to put himself right. The spectacle goes on, and we are told that this is a sign and a symbol of cleverness in the parliament of Canada. Well, Mr. Chairman, as far as I am concerned I think this item should pass. We can stay here for another hour, however, and let the people see the spectacle if hon. gentlemen opposite insist.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Prime
Minister is fond of using the expression "what a spectacle" and of referring to the amount of time consumed in unnecessary discussion. If my right hon. friend will take time to look over Hansard to-morrow he will be surprised to see the spectacle he has made of himself during this evening, and the amount of time he as Prime Minister has taken up in the house in regard to this one particular item, giving first one version, then another, none of them correlated or consistent one with the other.
May I make our position very dear. We are asked to vote $2,000,000, which is not a small sum, under a contract the terms of which are not known to this house at the present time.
You had them under your fingers for nine years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman's government has had them recently in the council chamber, and I venture to say he does not know anything about them.
You must be in the same boat; you do not know anything about them either.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is why
I am asking for them. The Prime Minister has said he does not know what they are; the Minister of Railways does not know the terms of the contract, and there is not an hon. member of this house who knows those terms. All we are asking now is to be permitted to see the contract in order to learn what are the terms.
But you voted money on it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, and it has been stated that we entered into the contract at the start. If a Liberal government entered into that contract, if I am not mistaken, it will be found that there is a clause in it providing that unless the moneys are appropriated by parliament they shall not be available for any of the work. And if that clause is there it furnishes a very good reason why my right hon. friend may not wish to produce the contract to-night or at any time. I am not asking him to discontinue the whole discussion until the contract is produced. I said fully an hour ago that I thought it would be well for the item to stand until the contract was produced, and I am still of the opinion that it should stand until then. Obviously it cannot be produced to-night. But there are a good many more estimates still to be discussed. If the Prime Minister refuses to produce the contract and wishes to have the discussion continue until it is produced, that must be his responsibility. We are anxious to facilitate the business of the house and get on with the items, but we are going to know the terms of that contract before we vote $2,000,000 under it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Had the request for the contract been made before six o'clock the contract would have been secured, but the staff of the Department of Railways and Canals does not work at night, and these contracts are treated as having some value. One of the deputies hearing the discussion this afternoon obtained a copy of the letter and also section 43 of the Porter contract which I read to the house, believing that these were the only important clauses to read. This matter must come before the house on the main estimates, and I will undertake to produce the contract and, if desired, have copies made before that time. But so far as this item is concerned I cannot see that it has reference to it at all. I do not think any purpose can be served, so far as the passing of this item is concerned, by the production of the contract, and it would be very much to be regretted if the House of Commons took the attitude of one party saying, "We will not go on until you produce the contract," and the other party saying, "We will." I am perfectly frank in saying that the house has a right to the contract and we shall be glad to table it. But I cannot produce it when I have no notice, and did not know that it would be called for, seeing that it is a contract which has been

Supply-Welland Canal
nine years in force and under which my hon. friends have voted very large sums of money indeed. The relevant section-at least the section which I thought relevant-the minister got one of the deputies to get for him. He sent word out as soon as the question was raised, hoping that he might procure it, but he has not got it. It cannot be produced at the moment. That is what I am informed. I shall be very glad indeed to lay on the table of the house copies of the Welland canal contracts, and before the main estimates are considered there will be ample opportunity to do so. The truth is, I am-sorry to say, that I treated these supplementary estimates for the year ending March 31, 1931, in perhaps a much more casual way than I should have because I had been under the impression that the expenditures having been made and the obligations incurred, parliament as a matter of course would authorize them. In connection with the main estimates there will be every opportunity for discussing any question involved, or giving any information desired. If I were in the position of the leader of the opposition I would endeavour to obtain all the information that might possibly be procurable ; but no one has ever heard me suggesting that we should ask for information with respect to a contract if it were merely a contract upon which payment had been made for seven or eight years. The time to do that is when the contract is first brought to the attention of the house, and usually this is done. I believe, in this case, the same thing occurred. The contract, I think, was made in August, 1921. Perhaps it was after the government came in, but I believe I read that it was made in August, 1921. That was one contract, because there are various contracts in connection with the various sections, bearing different dates. I can only say that the items are here and to-morrow is the last day in the fiscal year in which these moneys can be paid. That is all there is about it, and if the opposition takes the view that they should not be paid, we will endeavour to do the best we can. In the past, however, it has been customary to pass these estimates without much discussion. It is true the pages of Hansard will show that I took a great deal of space making explanations, but these explanations were made not because I desired to give them at length but because I was asked by the house itself to make them. And if the reasons I have given lack coherence I can only say that there were many considerations that led to our purpose, which we believed to be in the public interest, to vote the money to which the contractors are entitled.

My right hon. friend has made reference to some contract undertaken by one Mr. Marshall for which I am accused of getting a governor general's warrant to pay for the work done. He has not offered any explanation. I am bound to say I do not remember the matter at all, but if Mr. Marshall was paid by order in council, undoubtedly the government knew all about it, and I cannot see why my right hon. friend should at this time make reference to this particular question. So far as my memory serves me, I never asked the government to grant me a warrant which was not justified and necessary in the public interest. Let me say to my right hon. friend that if he expects to get estimates through he will find that the quickest way is to produce all papers asked for, or to allow an item to stand until they are produced. Nor was he recreant in his duty in asking ministers, when we were on that side, to produce papers before an item was passed. We are well within our rights in asking for all information and for all papers, and it will not hurt my right hon. friend to allow the item to stand until to-morrow, seeing that he still has a great many more items to pass.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The sage observations offered by my hon. friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) and the advice tendered may be most excellent; I fancy they are. But they have no application to this particular case, because this afternoon when the question was raised I asked that the item stand and I supplied in detail the information requested. Had the opposition asked for the production of the contracts they would have been here to-night. But we were not asked for their production.

No sage observations have been made. So far as I am personally concerned I do not like references to past actions on my part without full opportunity being given to review them, when an impression is left or sought to be left that there is something wrong somewhere about the transaction. I may say to my right hon. friend that any time he attempts that with me he will not get away with it without a reasonable explanation. There is nothing sage about that statement. May I observe, however, that he, himself, tendered some sage advice across the floor when we were sitting on the side he and his followers now occupy. And we were bound by what he at that time decided was in the best interests of the public-we produced whatever was asked for.
Supply-Welland Canal

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will have, produced from the files and laid on the table of the house, the original with respect to the matter. He brought the criticism on himself.

I have been listening with great care to the discussion that has been going on between the Prime Minister and the loader of the opposition. I have been doing my best to discover what the real issue is and (o endeavour to come to some conclusion respecting it. The whole spectacle this evening proves the contention I have often put forward in this house, that the committee of the whole is not a very good place in which to discuss any estimate. I hope some day we shall have more adequate facilities provided. It is significant that for very many years money has been voted by parliament in connection with the contract at present under discussion. The challenge that no one knows what is in that contract has been issued and no one has taken it up. Having voted so much money during all these years without knowing what is in the contract, I do not mind doing it once more. I do not see that we will be doing more harm than has been done already. To me all this discussion seems to be nothing more than red tape. The declaration has been made that this vote is irregular. If I understood the Prime Minister correctly, he said that it is not irregular, it has been done before by hon. gentlemen on this side. That has not been denied, and therefore I can only conclude that if it is irregular it has been done before. Having been done before, why not go ahead and be irregular some more? This discussion is simply red tape. The amount will have to be paid. If it is authorized by the contract it will have to be paid; if it is authorized by the government apart from the contract it will have to be paid, and so it does not make much difference to me personally whether we vote this to-night or to-morrow.
Something has been said about the authority of parliament being jeopardized by this vote.	Parliament never had any
authority except the authority of the governing party. That authority comes from the cabinet, and that has been the only authority exercised by this parliament ever sinice I entered this chamber. I see no reason why we should object to following the same system. Perhaps we should have a better one, but although I have contended for a change, the right hon. leader of the opposition did not see fit to bring that about when he was Prime Minister. I see no reason for holding up this vote, particularly when we are 
advised that under the contract the company was authorized to carry on because of unemployment conditions. We know that such conditions existed and we know that such work would give employment to many men. We know they got work and in view of that I think this is an excellent time for conciliation. I enjoyed the speech of the leader of the opposition on conciliation in connection with the Imperial conference; if that is good for the Imperial conference it is a most excellent thing for the parliament of Canada. Let us have some conciliation and let us have it now and get on with the business of the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The original Johnston P. Porter contract has been secured by the Minister of Railways and Canals. It being an original document, obviously it cannot be laid upon the table. However, I will pass it over to my right hon. friend. The contract which is dated August 18, 1021, was authorized by order in council dated August 18, 1021. It calls for tfhe construction of sections 1 and 2 of the Welland ship canal to be completed by March 31, 1025. Security of $400,000 was furnished. This matter is covered by departmental records file No. 14002, and the insurance policies required by section 125 were filed. The time for completion was extended to March 31, 1027, by a supplemental agreement which is attached to the contract. It was later extended to March 31, 1020, by order in council. It was again extended to June 30, 1030, by order in council dated March 16, 1020. It was finally extended to March 31, 1031, by a supplemental agreement dated January 8, 1031, which is attached to the contract.
A great deal of this information is new to us, especially that in connection with the supplemental agreement dated January 8, 1031.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is the same as those of 1027 and 1020.

Why have not we the
right to see that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not dispute the
hon. member's right to see it.
We have been told all afternoon that there was no new contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Neither there was.

I should say that a supplementary agreement would be very similar to a contract.

Supply-Welland Canal

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It merely extends the
time for completion.
It is a new condition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The time was extended.
Although it may have no great bearing, I think we have occasion to resent the right hon. gentleman's manner towards us during the course of the afternoon. No one on this side of the chamber had an idea other than that this contract had been authorized by order in council, and so we did not ask for its production.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The original oontract was authorized by order in council.

I am sorry if the right hon.
gentleman misunderstood me. When the matter was being under discussion this afternoon we were given to understand that this $2,000,000 vote was an amount authorized by order in council. Before six o'clock we did not ask for the production of the contract because ,we did not think it was necessary, but after the dinner recess the right hon. gentleman moved from one position to another. He then proceeded to cite one clause of the contract without laying the complete contract upon the table of the house as he should have done. He knows very well that had we raised a point *of order and asked the Chairman to require the production of the contract he would have been obliged under the rules of this house to produce it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think not.

As the right hon. gentleman thinks not, the next time a similar question .arises we will ask for a ruling from the Chairman. In any case it was only after the dinner .recess that this matter of a contract came up. A clause from the contract was cited and a letter was read, and now we find that there was a supplementary contract. I submit that events have shown that we were perfectly Justified in requesting the information which we have received from the right hon. gentleman. He has laid great stress upon the fact that this contract has been in existence for nine years, and that millions of dollars have Been voted under it, bu't I would call his -attention to the fact that on every occasion upon which moneys were voted on this contract there were in their seats some responsible ministers who were prepared to give explanations. To-night we had the right hon. minister stating that he knew nothing about a .contract; he gave us to understand that the Minister of Railways and Canals was not iamiliar with the details-the minister will 22110-29
correct me if I am wrong-and he said: You must vote the money under this because you have voted money already. I submit that we are entitled to differentiate between the manner in which this contract has been treated in other years and the manner in which it should be treated this year.
A further reference was made by the right hon. gentleman which might be rather annoying to hon. members on this side of the chamber. He has intimated that on the last days of the fiscal year we are endeavouring to obstruct or to retard the progress of this estimate. The right hon. gentleman could have brought these estimates down last week.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, he could not.
Why could he not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He could not bring them down until he obtained the consent of the house.

He could have obtained that consent last Monday; there was no necessity for waiting until the last days of the fiscal year in order to bring them down. We are being asked to vote $2,000,000 without having any information or without being permitted to have the documents to which we are entitled.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I thank my
right hon. friend for having produced this contract. The production is all the more remarkable because the Prime Minister told us only a moment ago that the vaults were locked and the clerks were in bed and therefore it was impossible to get anything. However, it is here and he has been kind enough to give it to us. I believe I have discovered the reason why my right hon. friend did not wish to produce this contract. The latest version with respect to the matter was that there was no order in council. I find here a definite contract reading:
This agreement made the 8th day of January, 1931, between Johnston P. Porter, of the city of Halifax, in the county of Halifax and province of Nova Scotia, of the first part, and His Majesty the King represented herein by the Minister of Railways and Canals of Canada, of the second part.
This is a formal contract signed by Mr. Porter, the contractor, and the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, but in this formal contract there is reference to an order in council in virtue of which this present contract has been entered into.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Is that not just an extension of the contract?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, but it is in virtue of an order in council granting an

Supply

Welland Canal

extension of time that it has been possible to make a new contract. I hope the hon. member for Wetaskiwin will not hold us lacking in any desire to be conciliatory when we are simply endeavouring to get at the terms of contracts which are for expenditures involving millions of dollars. One of the reasons given for this contract is as follows:
And whereas, under and by virtue of an order in council (P.C. 2303) dated the 30th September, 1930, authority has been given to the further extension of the time for the completion of the works contracted for under contract No. 24275, by the party of the first part, io the 31st day of March, 1931.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was not the order in council my right hon. friend was talking about.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is an order in council pertaining to the contract and in virtue of which the contract was made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In virtue of which the agreement respecting the $2,000,000 expenditure which we are being asked to make good to-night was entered into.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman's own government during its regime extended the contract three times, and since we came in we extended it once. This is just an extension of the contract. There is no change in it. The ex-Minister of Marine nods his head. He agrees with me.
It is quite right that we extended the contract.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I come to the original contract. We have now _an. order, in council which extends the time under which this work is to be done, an order in council of which the house up to this moment had received no information and of which it would have had no knowledge but for the production of the document in consequence of all the efforts we made this afternoon and evening to obtain it. In virtue of the extension of time given by order in council of September 30, the Minister of Railways and Canals subsequently had a contract entered into between the contractor and his deputy.
What is the date of the order in council?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The order in council extending the time is dated September 30, 1930, a rather significant date. After we had had the, special session of parliament, after parliament had voted $20,000,000 to aid unemployment, and after my right hon. friend had had an opportunity to ask parliament foi

any privilege or right which he wished to have with respect to meeting the unemployment situation, it is then that the government by order in council extends the time of this contract. Then we come to the month of December.
When the appropriation voted for that same year had expired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On September 30 there still was some of the appropriation, but after that the appropriation had expired-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The appropriation had
not expired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not the whole of it in September, but my right hon. friend and his colleagues were paving the way for this further amount to be authorized later on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Prime Minister was away.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not
imagine my right hon. friend's colleagues did anything without his full knowledge. Even if he were away, I think he knew all about it. But this agreement is dated the 8th day of January, 1931, a formal agreement signed by the contractor and the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Merely extending the
time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, authorizing further expenditures. This is not even the letter to which reference has been made. All we were told of was a letter written by the deputy; there was nothing about a new contract, but this is a contract, signed, sealed and delivered in the presence of Mr. F. S. Lazier for the party of the first part, and in the presence of Mr. J. Proulx for the party of the second part.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend read the operative part of it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I shall read
the whole of it. It reads:
This agreement made this 8th day of January, 1931, between Johnston P. Porter, of ;he city of Halifax, in the county of Halifax and province of Nova Scotia, of the first part, and His Majesty the King, represented herein by the Minister of Railways and Canals, of Canada, of the second part:
Witnesseth a contract bearing No. 24275, dated the 18th day of August, 1921 (hereinafter referred to as "contract No. 24275") was entered into by and between the party of the first part and the party of the second part for the construction and completion of sections Nos. 1 and 2 of the Welland Ship canal, for the considerations and subject to the terms, covenants,

Supply-Welland Canal
provisoes, agreements, conditions and reservations as in contract No. 24275 set out, which, by reference thereto, will at length and more fully .appear;
And whereas the time for the completion, by the party of the first part, of the works contracted for under contract No. 24275 was therein fixed for the 31st day of March, 1925, as in clause 3 of contract No. 24275 set out and provided;
And whereas the time for the completion of the works contracted for under contract No. 24275 was extended by supplemental agreement dated April 20, 1925, to the 31st day of March, 1927;
And whereas the time for the completion of the works contracted for under contract No. 24275 was further extended by order in council (P.C. 395) dated March 14, 1927, to the 31st day of March, 1929, and by order in council (P.C. 448) dated March 16, 1929, to the 30th day of June, 1930;
And whereas the party of the first part has not yet done, furnished, performed and delivered the works contracted for under contract No. 24275;
And whereas, under and by virtue of an order in council (P.C. 2303) dated the 30th day of September, 1930, authority has been given to the further extension of the time for the completion of the works contracted for under contract No. 24275, by the party of the first, part, to the 31st day of March, 1931.
Witnesseth that, in consideration of the premises, the parties hereto have mutually covenanted and agreed as follows:
1. That the time for the completion, as set and provided in clause 3 of the contract No. 24275, by the party of the first part for the party of the second part, of the works contracted for under contract No. 24275 and as extended by supplemental agreement and orders in council aforesaid is hereby further extended to the thirty-first day of March, 1931, and that each and all, except and subject as hereinbefore set out and provided, the terms, covenants, provisoes, agreements, conditions and reservations in contract No. 24275 set out and provided shall be and continue in force and effect between the parties hereto in as full and complete a manner as if the date (the 31st day of March, 1925) set out and provided in clause 3 of contract No. 24275 for the completion of the works contracted for under contract No. 24275 had been the 31st day of March, 1931 (the date herein named and fixed) named and fixed in contract No. 24275 in the first instance instead of the date therein so named and fixed.
In witness whereof the parties hereto have executed these presents the day and year first above written.
Signed, sealed a"nd delivered by the party of the first part in the presence of F. S. Lazier.
J. B. Porter.
Signed, sealed and delivered by the party of the second part in the presence of J. Proulx.
V. I. Smart,
Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals.
J. W. Pugsley,
Secretary.
In other words, the amount of $2,000,000, which we are now being asked to appropriate, is in virtue not of any estimates submitted 22110-29j
to the house by a previous administration nor of any act of a previous administration at all, but by virtue of an extension of time made by the government of the day opposite on the 30th September last and in virtue of a new contract entered into between the contractor and the present government in January of this year for which at the time there was no existing appropriation. That is the position. It is in respect of moneys that were not voted previously. May I quote to my right hon. friend what he himself had to say in parliament at the special session with respect to appropriations that had not received the sanction of parliament? He was referring to remarks of the ex-Minister of Justice in the debate on unemployment relief, and he will find his own words at page 91 of Hansard of the special session as follows:
Having regard to the attitude taken by the right hon. gentleman as to the desirability of having antecedent parliamentary sanction for expenditures-
Not post-parliamentary sanction of expenditures, but antecedent parliamentary sanction of expenditures such as we are now discussing.
-I am sure that he will agree that any effort to appropriate so substantial a sum as that mentioned in the resolution should have parliamentary sanction before the money is expended.
And my right hon. friend adds these words:
I think that is a cardinal principle of representative institutions and of responsible government.
Those are the words of the Prime Minister on the lilth of September, before this extension of time was granted with reference to this $2,000,000 contract that we are now discussing, and three or four months before the actual contract itself was entered into with the contractors for the additional $2,000,000. So I say to my right hon. friend that out of his own lips he stands condemned. I am prepared to leave the matter at that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Now that the contract has been produced, I do not intend to take up very much time beyond saying that the general principle upon which I have always proceeded is that there should be antecedent authorization by parliament of public expenditures. There was in this instance antecedent parliamentary authorization because parliament had approved of the contract and of its terms by voting money for the work for nine or ten years in succession. It will be remembered that this contract was to be fulfilled in March, 1925, and when the right
Supply-Welland Canal

hon. gentleman's government went out of power in July, 1930, the contract had not been completed. Therefore there were extensions, three in number, and a further extension was made until the 31st of March of this year. There had been an antecedent approval by parliament of the contract that involves this large expenditure, but parliament had voted part of the money only.
But not approval of the expenditure itself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Parliament had antecedently approved of the contract and of the whole of the expenditures that were to be made for the purpose of carrying into effect the terms of the contract. Only part of the money, however, had been voted. It would be incumbent upon the crown to make good the moneys due for the work that was performed. I am not going to discuss that further.
When the right hon. gentleman and those associated with him were so insistent that they had never done such a thing, might I ask them whether, in 1928-29, the government of that day did not authorize work on the Hudson Bay railway, and that it be proceeded with after the appropriation for the year had been expended? Afterwards the sum of $1,700,000 was included in the 192930 estimates for that work. Let hon. gentlemen look up the estimates and see. The situation that arose then was not one of grave unemployment. It was simply a question of carrying on the work, and the government of that day arranged to get the money without coming to parliament. The Canadian National Railways put up the money in the meantime and parliament voted the money later. That hon. gentlemen will find by looking at the estimates for those two years.
I have endeavoured with a good deal of difficulty to get the contract for the right hon. gentleman and his friends. There is nothing about this matter that is irregular or improper or in any way at variance with the principles which I laid down. That is the reason why in respect to some new works to which reference has been made expenditures were not carried on: because it was felt-I have a very strong opinion about it- that as some of these works could not be completed before the end of this month, no start should be made upon them, the moneys voted being wholly insufficient for the purpose. So instead of calling for tenders and letting contracts, we decided we would do the best we could under the circumstances

then existing, and I do not believe that there is any member of this house who will say that if the right hon. gentleman opposite and his friends were in power and confronted with the same situation he would not have extended the contract for the same purpose, to enable the contractor to complete his obligation within the time mentioned and to take care of the problem of unemployment.
My hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power), who has referred to the order in council, knows perfectly well that the order in council read this evening was not the order in council to which reference was made this afternoon, nor was there in point of fact any new contract made. There was merely an extension of time granted, the only change made being in the date fixed for the completion of the contract by March 31, 1931. If there has been any violation of the principles of responsible government or representative institutions it certainly has not been in this case, because all that was done was to permit the contractor to go forward and finish his work, and he had to finish it by March 31 anyway.

We were told that there was an order in council, and then we were told that there was no order in council.
